Whose slope is $\frac{dy}{dx}$ is $\begin{aligned} & Y-y=\frac{dy}{dx}(X-x) \\ \\ & \begin{aligned} & \text{Putting}Y=0 \Rightarrow X=x-\frac{y}{(\frac{dy}{dx})}t \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha=x-\frac{y}{(\frac{dy}{dx})} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$ and putting $X=0 \Rightarrow Y=y-x\frac{dy}{dx}$ $\Rightarrow \beta=y-x\frac{dy}{dx}$ $\because P$ divides $AB$ in $1:k$ $x=\frac{k\alpha+0}{k+1}\text{and}y=\frac{k \times 0+\beta}{k+1}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow x(k+1)=k(x-\frac{y}{\frac{dy}{dx}}) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow xk+x=xk-\frac{yk}{\frac{dy}{dx}} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x\frac{dy}{dx}=-yk \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \text{or}\int \frac{dy}{y}=-k \times \int \frac{1}{x}dx \\ \\ & \Rightarrow logy=-klogx+logC \\ \\ & \text{or}logy \times x^{k}=logC \\ \\ & \Rightarrow yx^{k}=C \\ \\ & \text{putting}x=1,y=1 \Rightarrow c=1 \\ \\ & \text{so}yx^{k}=1 \end{aligned}$ Putting $x=\frac{1}{10},y=100 \Rightarrow 100 \times (\frac{1}{100})^{k}=1 \Rightarrow k=2$ so $yx^{2}=1$ or $y=\frac{1}{x^{2}}$ Now $e^{\frac{dy}{dx}}=kx+\frac{k}{2}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=log_{e}(kx+\frac{k}{2})=log_{e}(2x+1)$ On integrating $\begin{aligned} & y=\int 1 \cdot log_{e}(2x+1)dx \\ \\ & =xlog_{e}(2x+1)-\int \frac{1 \times 2}{2x+1} \times xdx \\ \\ & =xlog_{e}(2x+1)-\int 1-\frac{1}{2x+1}dx \\ \\ & y=xlog_{e}(2x+1)-x+\frac{1}{2}log_{e}(2x+1)+c \end{aligned}$ Put $x=0,y=k=2 \Rightarrow c=2$ putting $x=1$ $\begin{aligned} & y(1)=log_{e}3-1+\frac{1}{2}log_{e}3+2=\frac{3}{2}log_{e}3-1+2 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 4y(1)=6log_{e}3+4 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 4y(1)-6log_{e}3=4 \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_text: I.F $=e^{\int \frac{5dx}{x(x^{5}+1)}}=e^{\int \frac{5x^{-6}dx}{(x^{-5}+1)}}$ Put, $1+x^{-5}=t \Rightarrow -5x^{-6}dx=dt$ $\therefore$ $e^{\int -\frac{dt}{t}}=e^{-lnt}=\frac{1}{t}=\frac{x^{5}}{1+x^{5}}$ $\begin{aligned} y \cdot \frac{x^{5}}{1+x^{5}} & =\int \frac{x^{5}}{(1+x^{5})} \times \frac{(1+x^{5})^{2}}{x^{7}}dx \\ \\ & =\int x^{3}dx+\int x^{-2}dx \end{aligned}$ $y \cdot \frac{x^{5}}{1+x^{5}}=\frac{x^{4}}{4}-\frac{1}{x}+c$ $\text{Given that:}x=1 \Rightarrow y=2$ $\begin{aligned} & 2 \cdot \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{4}-1+c \\ \\ & c=\frac{7}{4} \\ \\ & y \cdot \frac{x^{5}}{1+x^{5}}=\frac{x^{4}}{4}-\frac{1}{x}+\frac{7}{4} \\ \\ & \text{Now put,}x=2 \\ \\ & y \cdot (\frac{32}{33})=\frac{21}{4} \\ \\ & y=\frac{693}{128} \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html: Let $\alpha x=exp(x^{\beta}y^{\gamma})$ be the solution of the differential equation $2x^{2}ydy-(1-xy^{2})dx=0,x>0,y(2)=\sqrt{log_{e}2}$ . Then $\alpha+\beta-\gamma$ equals :
questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & 2x^{2}ydy-(1-xy^{2})dx=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 2x^{2}y\frac{dy}{dx}-1+xy^{2}=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 2y\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{1}{x^{2}}+\frac{y^{2}}{x}=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 2y\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{y^{2}}{x}=\frac{1}{x^{2}}\text{(L.D.E)} \\ \\ & Let,y^{2}=t \Rightarrow 2y\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dt}{dx} \\ \\ & \frac{dt}{dx}+\frac{t}{x}=\frac{1}{x^{2}} \\ \\ & \text{I.F}=e^{\int \frac{1}{x}dx}=x \end{aligned}$ So, the general solution is $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow t \times x=\int x \cdot \frac{1}{x^{2}}dx \\ \\ & \Rightarrow y^{2} \cdot x=lnx+c \\ \\ & \text{Also,y(2)}=\sqrt{log_{e}2} \\ \\ & log_{e}^{2}2=log_{e}2+c \Rightarrow c=log_{e}2 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow y^{2}x=lnx+ln2 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow y^{2}x=ln2x \\ \\ & 2x=exp(x^{1}y^{2}) \end{aligned}$ By compare it with given solution we get, $\begin{aligned} & \alpha=2,\beta=1,\gamma=2 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha+\beta-\gamma=2+1-2=1 \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_text: Differentiating both sides we get, $\begin{aligned} & f^{'}(x)+\frac{f(x)}{x}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+1}} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{y}{x}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+1}} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow IF=x \\ \\ & \Rightarrow yx=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{x}{\sqrt{x+1}}dx+c \\ \\ & \Rightarrow yx=\frac{1}{2}(\frac{(x+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}}-2(x+1)^{\frac{1}{2}})+c \\ \\ & xy=\frac{1}{3}(x+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}-(x+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}+c \\ \\ & f(3)=2 \end{aligned}$ So, $x=3,y=2$ $\Rightarrow c=\frac{16}{3}$ Now, $x=8$ $8f(8)=\frac{27}{3}-3+\frac{16}{3}=\frac{34}{3}$ $12f(8)=\frac{34}{3} \times \frac{12}{8}=17$

questions.explanation_text: Given, $y(x+1)dx-x^{2}dy=0$ $\Rightarrow (\frac{x+1}{x^{2}})dx=\frac{dy}{y}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{x}dx+\frac{dx}{x^{2}}=\frac{dy}{y}$ Integrating both sides, we get $\int \frac{dx}{x}+\int \frac{dx}{x^{2}}=\int \frac{dy}{y}$ $\Rightarrow ln|x|-\frac{1}{x}=ln|y|+C$ ..... (1) Given $y(1)=e$ $\therefore$ $x=1$ and $y=e$ Putting value of x and y in equation (1), we get $ln|1|-\frac{1}{1}=ln|e|+C$ $\Rightarrow 0-1=1+C$ $\Rightarrow C=-2$ $\therefore$ Equation (1) becomes, $ln|x|=-\frac{1}{x}=ln|y|-2$ $\Rightarrow ln|y|=ln|x|-\frac{1}{x}+2$ $\Rightarrow y=e^{ln|x|}.e^{2-\frac{1}{x}}$ $\Rightarrow y=x.e^{2-\frac{1}{x}}$ Now, $\underset{x \rightarrow 0^{+}}{lim}y$ $=\underset{x \rightarrow 0^{+}}{lim}(x.e^{2-\frac{1}{x}})$ $=0.e^{-\alpha}$ $=0$
questions.explanation_html:
Given,

$y(x+1)dx-x^{2}dy=0$

$\Rightarrow (\frac{x+1}{x^{2}})dx=\frac{dy}{y}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{x}dx+\frac{dx}{x^{2}}=\frac{dy}{y}$

Integrating both sides, we get

$\int \frac{dx}{x}+\int \frac{dx}{x^{2}}=\int \frac{dy}{y}$

$\Rightarrow ln|x|-\frac{1}{x}=ln|y|+C$ ..... (1)

Given $y(1)=e$

$\therefore$ $x=1$ and $y=e$

Putting value of x and y in equation (1), we get

$ln|1|-\frac{1}{1}=ln|e|+C$

$\Rightarrow 0-1=1+C$

$\Rightarrow C=-2$

$\therefore$ Equation (1) becomes,

$ln|x|=-\frac{1}{x}=ln|y|-2$

$\Rightarrow ln|y|=ln|x|-\frac{1}{x}+2$

$\Rightarrow y=e^{ln|x|}.e^{2-\frac{1}{x}}$

$\Rightarrow y=x.e^{2-\frac{1}{x}}$

Now,

$\underset{x \rightarrow 0^{+}}{lim}y$

$=\underset{x \rightarrow 0^{+}}{lim}(x.e^{2-\frac{1}{x}})$

$=0.e^{-\alpha}$

$=0$

questions.explanation_text: $x^{3}dy+xydx-dx=0$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1-xy}{x^{3}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{y}{x^{2}}=\frac{1}{x^{3}}$ I.F. $=e^{\int \frac{dx}{x^{2}}}=e^{-\frac{1}{x}}$ $\therefore ye^{-\frac{1}{x}}=\int \frac{e^{-\frac{1}{x}}}{x^{3}}dx$ For RHS put $-\frac{1}{x}=t \Rightarrow \frac{dx}{x^{2}}=dt$ $\therefore ye^{-\frac{1}{x}}=-\int te^{t}dt$ $\Rightarrow ye^{-\frac{1}{x}}=-[te^{t}-e^{t}]+c$ $\Rightarrow ye^{-\frac{1}{x}}=\frac{e^{-\frac{1}{x}}}{x}+e^{-\frac{1}{x}}+c$ $↓y(\frac{1}{2})=3-e$ $\Rightarrow (3-e)e^{-2}=2e^{-2}+e^{-2}+c$ $\Rightarrow c=-\frac{1}{e}$ For $y(1)$ put $x=1,c=-e^{-1}$ in equation (i) we get $ye^{-1}=e^{-1}+e^{-1}-e^{-1}$ $\Rightarrow y=1$
questions.explanation_html:
$x^{3}dy+xydx-dx=0$

$\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1-xy}{x^{3}}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{y}{x^{2}}=\frac{1}{x^{3}}$

I.F. $=e^{\int \frac{dx}{x^{2}}}=e^{-\frac{1}{x}}$

$\therefore ye^{-\frac{1}{x}}=\int \frac{e^{-\frac{1}{x}}}{x^{3}}dx$

For RHS put $-\frac{1}{x}=t \Rightarrow \frac{dx}{x^{2}}=dt$

$\therefore ye^{-\frac{1}{x}}=-\int te^{t}dt$

$\Rightarrow ye^{-\frac{1}{x}}=-[te^{t}-e^{t}]+c$

$\Rightarrow ye^{-\frac{1}{x}}=\frac{e^{-\frac{1}{x}}}{x}+e^{-\frac{1}{x}}+c$

$↓y(\frac{1}{2})=3-e$

$\Rightarrow (3-e)e^{-2}=2e^{-2}+e^{-2}+c$

$\Rightarrow c=-\frac{1}{e}$

For $y(1)$ put $x=1,c=-e^{-1}$ in equation (i) we get $ye^{-1}=e^{-1}+e^{-1}-e^{-1}$

$\Rightarrow y=1$

If $x(\frac{\pi}{6})=\frac{1}{log_{e}m-log_{e}n}$ , where $m$ and $n$ are coprime, then $mn$ is equal to __________.
questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & (cosy)(ln(cosy))^{2}dx=(1+3xlncosy)sinydy \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{(1+3xlncosy)siny}{(lncosy)^{2}cosy} \\ \\ & =tany[\frac{1}{(lncosy)^{2}}+\frac{3x}{lncosy}] \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{dx}{dy}-(\frac{3tany}{lncosy})x=\frac{tany}{(lncosy)^{2}} \end{aligned}$ Which is a linear differential equation. $\text{I.F.}=e^{-\int \frac{3tany}{lncosy}dy}=(lncosy)^{3}$ So, the solution is : $\begin{aligned} & x \times (lncosy)^{3}=\int ((lncosy)^{3} \times \frac{tany}{(lncosy)^{2}})dy \\ \\ & x \times (lncosy)^{3}=\frac{-(lncosy)^{2}}{2}+C \end{aligned}$ $\text{At}y=\frac{\pi}{3}\text{,}$ $\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{2ln2} \times (ln(\frac{1}{2}))^{3}=-\frac{(ln(\frac{1}{2}))^{2}}{2}+C \\ \\ & \Rightarrow C=0 \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \text{So,}x \times ln^{3}cosy=\frac{-ln^{2}cosy}{2} \\ \\ & \text{At}y=\frac{\pi}{6},x \times (ln(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}))^{3}=-\frac{1}{2}(ln(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}))^{2} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x=-\frac{1}{2ln(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & =-\frac{1}{2[ln\sqrt{3}-ln2]}=\frac{-1}{2[\frac{1}{2}ln3-ln2]} \\ \\ & =\frac{-1}{2[\frac{ln3-ln4}{2}]}=\frac{1}{ln4-ln3} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow m=4,n=3 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow mn=12 \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & (cosy)(ln(cosy))^{2}dx=(1+3xlncosy)sinydy \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{(1+3xlncosy)siny}{(lncosy)^{2}cosy} \\ \\ & =tany[\frac{1}{(lncosy)^{2}}+\frac{3x}{lncosy}] \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{dx}{dy}-(\frac{3tany}{lncosy})x=\frac{tany}{(lncosy)^{2}} \end{aligned}$

Which is a linear differential equation.

$\text{I.F.}=e^{-\int \frac{3tany}{lncosy}dy}=(lncosy)^{3}$

So, the solution is :

$\begin{aligned} & x \times (lncosy)^{3}=\int ((lncosy)^{3} \times \frac{tany}{(lncosy)^{2}})dy \\ \\ & x \times (lncosy)^{3}=\frac{-(lncosy)^{2}}{2}+C \end{aligned}$

$\text{At}y=\frac{\pi}{3}\text{,}$

$\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{2ln2} \times (ln(\frac{1}{2}))^{3}=-\frac{(ln(\frac{1}{2}))^{2}}{2}+C \\ \\ & \Rightarrow C=0 \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \text{So,}x \times ln^{3}cosy=\frac{-ln^{2}cosy}{2} \\ \\ & \text{At}y=\frac{\pi}{6},x \times (ln(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}))^{3}=-\frac{1}{2}(ln(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}))^{2} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x=-\frac{1}{2ln(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & =-\frac{1}{2[ln\sqrt{3}-ln2]}=\frac{-1}{2[\frac{1}{2}ln3-ln2]} \\ \\ & =\frac{-1}{2[\frac{ln3-ln4}{2}]}=\frac{1}{ln4-ln3} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow m=4,n=3 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow mn=12 \end{aligned}$

Let $x=x(y)$ be the solution of the differential equation

$2(y+2)log_{e}(y+2)dx+(x+4-2log_{e}(y+2))dy=0,y>-1$

with $x(e^{4}-2)=1$ . Then $x(e^{9}-2)$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & 2(y+2)ln(y+2)dx+(x+4-2ln(y+2))dy=0 \\ \\ & 2ln(y+2)+(x+4-2ln(y+2))\frac{1}{y+2} \cdot \frac{dy}{dx}=0 \\ \\ & \text{let,}ln(y+2)=t \\ \\ & \frac{1}{y+2} \cdot \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dt}{dx} \\ \\ & 2t+(x+4-2t) \cdot \frac{dt}{dx}=0 \\ \\ & (x+4-2t)\frac{dt}{dx}=-2t \\ \\ & \frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{2t-4-x}{2t} \\ \\ & \frac{dx}{dt}+\frac{x}{2t}=\frac{2t-4}{2t} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & x \cdot t^{1/2}=\int \frac{2t-4}{2t} \cdot t^{1/2} \cdot dt \\ \\ & x \cdot t^{1/2}=\int (t^{1/2}-\frac{2}{t^{1/2}}) \cdot dt \\ \\ & =\frac{t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}}-2 \cdot \frac{t^{\frac{1}{2}}}{\frac{1}{2}}+C \\ \\ & x \cdot t^{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{2t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}-4t^{\frac{1}{2}}+C \\ \\ & x=\frac{2}{3} \cdot t-4+C \cdot t^{\frac{-1}{2}} \\ \\ & x=\frac{2}{3}ln(y+2)-4+C \cdot (ln(y+2))^{\frac{-1}{2}} \end{aligned}$ Put $y=e^{4}-2,x=1$ $\begin{aligned} & 1=\frac{2}{3} \times 4-4+C \times \frac{1}{2} \\ \\ & \frac{C}{2}=5-\frac{8}{3}=\frac{7}{3} \\ \\ & C=\frac{14}{3} \\ \\ & x=\frac{2}{3} \times 9-4+\frac{14}{3} \times \frac{1}{3} \\ \\ & =2+\frac{14}{9} \\ \\ & =\frac{32}{9} \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html:
Let $y=y(x)$ be a solution curve of the differential equation.

$(1-x^{2}y^{2})dx=ydx+xdy$ .

If the line $x=1$ intersects the curve $y=y(x)$ at $y=2$ and the line $x=2$ intersects the curve $y=y(x)$ at $y=\alpha$ , then a value of $\alpha$ is :
questions.explanation_text: We have, $\begin{aligned} & (1-x^{2}y^{2})dx=ydx+xdy,y(1)=2 \\ \\ & dx=\frac{ydx+xdy}{1-(xy)^{2}} \end{aligned}$ On integrating both sides, we get $\begin{aligned} \int dx & =\int \frac{d(xy)}{1-(xy)^{2}} \\ \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}log|\frac{1+xy}{1-xy}|+C \end{aligned}$ As, $y(1)=2$ $\begin{aligned} 1 & =\frac{1}{2}log|\frac{1+2}{1-2}|+C \\ \\ \Rightarrow C & =1-\frac{1}{2}log3 \end{aligned}$ Now, substitute $x=2$ as $y(2)=\alpha$ $2=\frac{1}{2}log|\frac{1+2\alpha}{1-2\alpha}|+1-\frac{1}{2}log3$ $\begin{aligned} 1+\frac{1}{2}log3 & =\frac{1}{2}log|\frac{1+2\alpha}{1-2\alpha}| \\ \\ 2+log3 & =log|\frac{1+2\alpha}{1-2\alpha}| \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{1+2\alpha}{1-2\alpha}|=3e^{2} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{1+2\alpha}{1-2\alpha}= \pm \frac{3e^{2}}{1} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2\alpha}=\frac{\pm 3e^{2}+1}{\pm 3e^{2}-1} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 2\alpha=\frac{\pm 3e^{2}-1}{\pm 3e^{2}+1} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \alpha=\frac{1}{2}(\frac{\pm 3e^{2}-1}{1 \pm 3e^{2}}) \\ \\ \therefore \alpha=\frac{3e^{2}-1}{2(1+3e^{2})}\text{or}\frac{3e^{2}+1}{2(3e^{2}-1)} \end{aligned}$

We have,

$\begin{aligned} & (1-x^{2}y^{2})dx=ydx+xdy,y(1)=2 \\ \\ & dx=\frac{ydx+xdy}{1-(xy)^{2}} \end{aligned}$

On integrating both sides, we get

$\begin{aligned} \int dx & =\int \frac{d(xy)}{1-(xy)^{2}} \\ \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}log|\frac{1+xy}{1-xy}|+C \end{aligned}$

As, $y(1)=2$

$\begin{aligned} 1 & =\frac{1}{2}log|\frac{1+2}{1-2}|+C \\ \\ \Rightarrow C & =1-\frac{1}{2}log3 \end{aligned}$

Now, substitute $x=2$ as $y(2)=\alpha$

$2=\frac{1}{2}log|\frac{1+2\alpha}{1-2\alpha}|+1-\frac{1}{2}log3$

$\begin{aligned} 1+\frac{1}{2}log3 & =\frac{1}{2}log|\frac{1+2\alpha}{1-2\alpha}| \\ \\ 2+log3 & =log|\frac{1+2\alpha}{1-2\alpha}| \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{1+2\alpha}{1-2\alpha}|=3e^{2} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{1+2\alpha}{1-2\alpha}= \pm \frac{3e^{2}}{1} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2\alpha}=\frac{\pm 3e^{2}+1}{\pm 3e^{2}-1} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 2\alpha=\frac{\pm 3e^{2}-1}{\pm 3e^{2}+1} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \alpha=\frac{1}{2}(\frac{\pm 3e^{2}-1}{1 \pm 3e^{2}}) \\ \\ \therefore \alpha=\frac{3e^{2}-1}{2(1+3e^{2})}\text{or}\frac{3e^{2}+1}{2(3e^{2}-1)} \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html: If the solution curve of the differential equation $(y-2log_{e}x)dx+(xlog_{e}x^{2})dy=0,x>1$ passes through the points $(e,\frac{4}{3})$ and $(e^{4},\alpha)$ , then $\alpha$ is equal to ____________.
questions.explanation_text: The given differential equation is, $\begin{aligned} & (y-2logx)dx+(xlogx^{2})dy=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{(2logx-y)}{2xlogx} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{y}{2xlogx}=\frac{1}{x} \end{aligned}$ It is a linear differential equation. $\therefore \text{I.F.}=e^{\int \frac{1}{2xlogx}dx}$ Put $logx=t \Rightarrow \frac{1}{x}dx=dt$ $\therefore \text{I.F.}=e^{\int \frac{1}{2t}dt}=e^{log(t)^{\frac{1}{2}}}=\sqrt{t}=\sqrt{logx}$ So, required solution is, $\begin{aligned} & y\sqrt{logx}=\int \frac{\sqrt{logx}}{x}dx \\ \\ & logx=v \Rightarrow \frac{1}{x}dx=dv \\ \\ & \Rightarrow y\sqrt{logx}=\int \sqrt{v}dv+C \\ \\ & \Rightarrow y\sqrt{logx}=\frac{2v^{3/2}}{3}+C \\ \\ & \Rightarrow y\sqrt{logx}=\frac{2}{3}(logx)^{3/2}+C \end{aligned}$ Now, this curve passes through $(e,\frac{4}{3})$ and $(e^{4},\alpha)$ $\begin{aligned} & \therefore \frac{4}{3}\sqrt{loge}=\frac{2}{3}(loge)^{3/2}+C \\ \\ & \Rightarrow C=\frac{4}{3}-\frac{2}{3}=\frac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$ Also, $\alpha\sqrt{loge^{4}}=\frac{2}{3}(loge^{4})^{3/2}+\frac{2}{3}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow 2\alpha=\frac{2}{3} \times (4)^{3/2}+\frac{2}{3}=\frac{16}{3}+\frac{2}{3}=\frac{18}{3} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha=3 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
The given differential equation is,

$\begin{aligned} & (y-2logx)dx+(xlogx^{2})dy=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{(2logx-y)}{2xlogx} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{y}{2xlogx}=\frac{1}{x} \end{aligned}$

It is a linear differential equation.

$\therefore \text{I.F.}=e^{\int \frac{1}{2xlogx}dx}$

Put $logx=t \Rightarrow \frac{1}{x}dx=dt$

$\therefore \text{I.F.}=e^{\int \frac{1}{2t}dt}=e^{log(t)^{\frac{1}{2}}}=\sqrt{t}=\sqrt{logx}$

So, required solution is,

$\begin{aligned} & y\sqrt{logx}=\int \frac{\sqrt{logx}}{x}dx \\ \\ & logx=v \Rightarrow \frac{1}{x}dx=dv \\ \\ & \Rightarrow y\sqrt{logx}=\int \sqrt{v}dv+C \\ \\ & \Rightarrow y\sqrt{logx}=\frac{2v^{3/2}}{3}+C \\ \\ & \Rightarrow y\sqrt{logx}=\frac{2}{3}(logx)^{3/2}+C \end{aligned}$

Now, this curve passes through $(e,\frac{4}{3})$ and $(e^{4},\alpha)$

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore \frac{4}{3}\sqrt{loge}=\frac{2}{3}(loge)^{3/2}+C \\ \\ & \Rightarrow C=\frac{4}{3}-\frac{2}{3}=\frac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$

Also, $\alpha\sqrt{loge^{4}}=\frac{2}{3}(loge^{4})^{3/2}+\frac{2}{3}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow 2\alpha=\frac{2}{3} \times (4)^{3/2}+\frac{2}{3}=\frac{16}{3}+\frac{2}{3}=\frac{18}{3} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha=3 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html: Let $y=y_{1}(x)$ and $y=y_{2}(x)$ be the solution curves of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}=y+7$ with initial conditions $y_{1}(0)=0$ and $y_{2}(0)=1$ respectively. Then the curves $y=y_{1}(x)$ and $y=y_{2}(x)$ intersect at

questions.explanation_text: The given differential equation is $\frac{dy}{dx}=y+7$ This is a first order linear differential equation and can be solved using an integrating factor. Rearrange the equation to the standard form of a linear differential equation : $\frac{dy}{dx}-y=7$ The integrating factor is $e^{-\int dx}=e^{-x}$ . Multiplying each side of the equation by the integrating factor gives : $e^{-x}\frac{dy}{dx}-e^{-x}y=7e^{-x}$ The left-hand side of the equation is the derivative of $(e^{-x}y)$ with respect to $x$ . So we can write the equation as : $\frac{d}{dx}(e^{-x}y)=7e^{-x}$ Integrate both sides with respect to $x$ : $e^{-x}y=-7e^{-x}+C$ Multiply both sides by $e^{x}$ to isolate $y$ : $y=-7+Ce^{x}$ So, the general solution to the differential equation is $y=-7+Ce^{x}$ . Now, let's apply the initial conditions to find the particular solutions : For $y_{1}(0)=0$ , we substitute into the general solution and solve for $C$ : $0=-7+C$ So, $C=7$ , and the solution for $y_{1}$ is $y_{1}(x)=7e^{x}-7$ . For $y_{2}(0)=1$ , again substitute into the general solution: $1=-7+C$ So, $C=8$ , and the solution for $y_{2}$ is $y_{2}(x)=8e^{x}-7$ . The two curves intersect when $y_{1}(x)=y_{2}(x)$ . Setting these equal and solving for $x$ gives : $7e^{x}-7=8e^{x}-7$ $e^{x}=0$ But $e^{x}=0$ has no solution, because the exponential function never equals zero. So, the curves $y=y_{1}(x)$ and $y=y_{2}(x)$ do not intersect at any point.
questions.explanation_html:
The given differential equation is

$\frac{dy}{dx}=y+7$

This is a first order linear differential equation and can be solved using an integrating factor.

Rearrange the equation to the standard form of a linear differential equation :

$\frac{dy}{dx}-y=7$

The integrating factor is $e^{-\int dx}=e^{-x}$ .

Multiplying each side of the equation by the integrating factor gives :

$e^{-x}\frac{dy}{dx}-e^{-x}y=7e^{-x}$

The left-hand side of the equation is the derivative of $(e^{-x}y)$ with respect to $x$ . So we can write the equation as :

$\frac{d}{dx}(e^{-x}y)=7e^{-x}$

Integrate both sides with respect to $x$ :

$e^{-x}y=-7e^{-x}+C$

Multiply both sides by $e^{x}$ to isolate $y$ :

$y=-7+Ce^{x}$

So, the general solution to the differential equation is $y=-7+Ce^{x}$ .

Now, let's apply the initial conditions to find the particular solutions :

For $y_{1}(0)=0$ , we substitute into the general solution and solve for $C$ :

$0=-7+C$

So, $C=7$ , and the solution for $y_{1}$ is $y_{1}(x)=7e^{x}-7$ .

For $y_{2}(0)=1$ , again substitute into the general solution:

$1=-7+C$

So, $C=8$ , and the solution for $y_{2}$ is $y_{2}(x)=8e^{x}-7$ .

The two curves intersect when $y_{1}(x)=y_{2}(x)$ . Setting these equal and solving for $x$ gives :

$7e^{x}-7=8e^{x}-7$

$e^{x}=0$

But $e^{x}=0$ has no solution, because the exponential function never equals zero.

So, the curves $y=y_{1}(x)$ and $y=y_{2}(x)$ do not intersect at any point.

questions.question_html: Let $f$ be a differentiable function such that $x^{2}f(x)-x=4\int_{0}^{x}tf(t)dt$ , $f(1)=\frac{2}{3}$ . Then $18f(3)$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Given that $x^{2}f(x)-x=4\int_{0}^{x}tf(t)dt$ On differentiating both sides with respect to $x$ , we get $\begin{aligned} & 2xf(x)+x^{2}f^{'}(x)-1=4xf(x) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x^{2}f^{'}(x)-2xf(x)-1=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x^{2}\frac{dy}{dx}-2xy=1(Let,y=f(x)] \\ \\ & \frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{2}{x}y=\frac{1}{x^{2}} \end{aligned}$ On comparing above equation with $\frac{dy}{dx}+Py=Q$ , where $P=-\frac{2}{x},Q=\frac{1}{x^{2}}$ Now, IF $=e^{\int (-2/x)dx}=e^{-2logx}=1/x^{2}$ Solution is $y(\frac{1}{x^{2}})=\int (\frac{1}{x^{2}})\frac{1}{x^{2}}dx$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{y}{x^{2}}=\int \frac{1}{x^{4}}dx \Rightarrow \frac{y}{x^{2}}=-\frac{1}{3x^{3}}+C \\ \\ & \Rightarrow y=-\frac{1}{3x}+Cx^{2} \end{aligned}$ Given, $f(1)=\frac{2}{3}$ . So, $\frac{2}{3}=-\frac{1}{3}+C \Rightarrow C=1$ Thus, $y=f(x)=-\frac{1}{3x}+x^{2}$ $\therefore 18f(3)=18{9-\frac{1}{9}}=18 \times \frac{80}{9}=160$

Given that

$x^{2}f(x)-x=4\int_{0}^{x}tf(t)dt$

On differentiating both sides with respect to $x$ , we get

$\begin{aligned} & 2xf(x)+x^{2}f^{'}(x)-1=4xf(x) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x^{2}f^{'}(x)-2xf(x)-1=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x^{2}\frac{dy}{dx}-2xy=1(Let,y=f(x)] \\ \\ & \frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{2}{x}y=\frac{1}{x^{2}} \end{aligned}$

On comparing above equation with

$\frac{dy}{dx}+Py=Q$ , where $P=-\frac{2}{x},Q=\frac{1}{x^{2}}$

Now, IF $=e^{\int (-2/x)dx}=e^{-2logx}=1/x^{2}$

Solution is $y(\frac{1}{x^{2}})=\int (\frac{1}{x^{2}})\frac{1}{x^{2}}dx$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{y}{x^{2}}=\int \frac{1}{x^{4}}dx \Rightarrow \frac{y}{x^{2}}=-\frac{1}{3x^{3}}+C \\ \\ & \Rightarrow y=-\frac{1}{3x}+Cx^{2} \end{aligned}$

Given, $f(1)=\frac{2}{3}$ .

So, $\frac{2}{3}=-\frac{1}{3}+C \Rightarrow C=1$

Thus, $y=f(x)=-\frac{1}{3x}+x^{2}$

$\therefore 18f(3)=18{9-\frac{1}{9}}=18 \times \frac{80}{9}=160$

$\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{3x^{5}tan^{-1}(x^{3})}{(1+x^{6})^{\frac{3}{2}}}y=2xexp{\frac{x^{3}-tan^{-1}x^{3}}{\sqrt{1+x^{6}}}}$

$IF=e^{-\int \frac{3x^{5}tan^{-1}(x^{3})}{(1+x^{6})^{\frac{3}{2}}}dx}$

Let $tan^{-1}x^{3}=t \Rightarrow \frac{3x^{2}}{1+x^{6}}dx=dt$

$\Rightarrow IF=e^{-\int \frac{tant}{sect}.tdt}=e^{-\int sint.tdt}=e^{tcost-sint}$

$\Rightarrow IF=e^{\frac{tan^{-1}(x^{3})}{\sqrt{1+x^{6}}}-\frac{x^{3}}{\sqrt{1+x^{6}}}}$

$\therefore$ Solution is

$y.e^{\frac{tan^{-1}x^{3}}{\sqrt{1+x^{6}}}-\frac{x^{3}}{\sqrt{1+x^{6}}}}=\int 2xdx+c$

$\Rightarrow y.e^{\frac{tan^{-1}x^{3}-x^{3}}{\sqrt{1+x^{6}}}}=x^{2}+c$

$y(0)=0 \Rightarrow c=0$

$x=1$

$y.e^{\frac{\frac{\pi}{4}-1}{\sqrt{2}}}=1$

$\Rightarrow y=e^{\frac{1-\frac{\pi}{4}}{\sqrt{2}}}$

$\Rightarrow y=e^{\frac{4-\pi}{4\sqrt{2}}}$

questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & \frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{y}{x}=y^{3}(1+log_{e}x) \\ \\ & \frac{1}{y^{3}}\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{1}{xy^{2}}=1+log_{e}x \\ \\ & \text{Let}-\frac{1}{y^{2}}=t \Rightarrow \frac{2}{y^{3}}\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dt}{dx} \\ \\ & \therefore \frac{dt}{dx}+\frac{2t}{x}=2(1+log_{e}x) \\ \\ & \text{I.F.}=e^{\int \frac{2}{x}dx}=x^{2} \\ \\ & \frac{-x^{2}}{y^{2}}=\frac{2}{3}((1+log_{e}x)x^{3}-\frac{x^{3}}{3})+C \\ \\ & y(1)=3 \\ \\ & \frac{y^{2}}{9}=\frac{C}{5-2x^{3}(2+log_{e}x^{3})} \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html:
If $y=y(x)$ is the solution of the differential equation

$\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{4x}{(x^{2}-1)}y=\frac{x+2}{(x^{2}-1)^{\frac{5}{2}}},x>1$ such that

$y(2)=\frac{2}{9}log_{e}(2+\sqrt{3})\text{and}y(\sqrt{2})=\alpha log_{e}(\sqrt{\alpha}+\beta)+\beta-\sqrt{\gamma},\alpha,\beta,\gamma \in ℕ\text{, then}\alpha\beta\gamma\text{is equal to}$ :
questions.explanation_text: We can solve the given differential equation using an integrating factor. The integrating factor is given by : $\mu(x)=e^{\int \frac{4x}{x^{2}-1}dx}=e^{2ln(x^{2}-1)}=(x^{2}-1)^{2}$ Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $\mu(x)$ , we get : $(x^{2}-1)^{2}\frac{dy}{dx}+4xy=\frac{x+2}{(x^{2}-1)^{\frac{1}{2}}}$ We can rewrite the left-hand side using the product rule: $\frac{d}{dx}((x^{2}-1)^{2}y)=\frac{x+2}{(x^{2}-1)^{\frac{1}{2}}}$ Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ , we get: $(x^{2}-1)^{2}y=\int \frac{x+2}{(x^{2}-1)^{\frac{1}{2}}}dx=\sqrt{x^{2}-1}+2ln|x+\sqrt{x^{2}-1}|+C$ where $C$ is the constant of integration. Using the initial condition $y(2)=\frac{2}{9}log_{e}(2+\sqrt{3})$ , we can solve for $C$ : At $x=2$ , $9 \cdot \frac{2}{9}ln(2+\sqrt{3})=2ln(2+\sqrt{3})+\sqrt{3}+C$ $C=-\sqrt{3}$ At $x=\sqrt{2}$ $y(\sqrt{2})=2ln(1+\sqrt{2})+1-\sqrt{3}$ $\beta=1,\alpha=2,\gamma=3$ $\Rightarrow \alpha\beta\gamma=6$
questions.explanation_html:
We can solve the given differential equation using an integrating factor.

The integrating factor is given by :

$\mu(x)=e^{\int \frac{4x}{x^{2}-1}dx}=e^{2ln(x^{2}-1)}=(x^{2}-1)^{2}$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $\mu(x)$ , we get :

$(x^{2}-1)^{2}\frac{dy}{dx}+4xy=\frac{x+2}{(x^{2}-1)^{\frac{1}{2}}}$

We can rewrite the left-hand side using the product rule:

$\frac{d}{dx}((x^{2}-1)^{2}y)=\frac{x+2}{(x^{2}-1)^{\frac{1}{2}}}$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ , we get:

$(x^{2}-1)^{2}y=\int \frac{x+2}{(x^{2}-1)^{\frac{1}{2}}}dx=\sqrt{x^{2}-1}+2ln|x+\sqrt{x^{2}-1}|+C$

where $C$ is the constant of integration. Using the initial condition $y(2)=\frac{2}{9}log_{e}(2+\sqrt{3})$ , we can solve for $C$ :

At $x=2$ ,

$9 \cdot \frac{2}{9}ln(2+\sqrt{3})=2ln(2+\sqrt{3})+\sqrt{3}+C$

$C=-\sqrt{3}$

At $x=\sqrt{2}$

$y(\sqrt{2})=2ln(1+\sqrt{2})+1-\sqrt{3}$

$\beta=1,\alpha=2,\gamma=3$

$\Rightarrow \alpha\beta\gamma=6$

questions.question_text: Let $y=y(x)$ be a solution of the differential equation $(xcosx)dy+(xysinx+ycosx-1)dx=0,0<x<\frac{\pi}{2}$ . If $\frac{\pi}{3}y(\frac{\pi}{3})=\sqrt{3}$ , then $|\frac{\pi}{6}y^{''}(\frac{\pi}{6})+2y^{'}(\frac{\pi}{6})|$ is equal to ____________.
questions.question_html: Let $y=y(x)$ be a solution of the differential equation $(xcosx)dy+(xysinx+ycosx-1)dx=0,0<x<\frac{\pi}{2}$ . If $\frac{\pi}{3}y(\frac{\pi}{3})=\sqrt{3}$ , then $|\frac{\pi}{6}y^{''}(\frac{\pi}{6})+2y^{'}(\frac{\pi}{6})|$ is equal to ____________.
questions.explanation_text: Given, differential equation $\begin{aligned} & (xcosx)dy+(xysinx+ycosx-1)dx=0,0<x<\frac{\pi}{2} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{xysinx+ycosx-1}{xcosx}=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}+(\frac{xysinx+ycosx}{xcosx})=\frac{1}{xcosx} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}+(tanx+\frac{1}{x})y=\frac{1}{xcosx} \end{aligned}$ Which is linear differential equation in the form of $\begin{aligned} & \frac{dy}{dx}+Py=Q \\ \\ & \therefore IF=e^{\int (tanx+\frac{1}{x})dx}=e^{(logsecx+logx)}=e^{log(xsecx)}=xsecx \end{aligned}$ $\therefore$ The general solution of the given differential equation $\begin{aligned} y \cdot IF=\int (Q \times IF)dx+c \\ \\ \Rightarrow y(xsecx)=\int (\frac{1}{xcosx}xsecx)dx+c \\ \\ \Rightarrow xysecx=\int sec^{2}xdx+c \\ \\ \Rightarrow xysecx=tanx+c........(i) \end{aligned}$ Since, $\frac{\pi}{3}y(\frac{\pi}{3})=\sqrt{3} \Rightarrow y(\frac{\pi}{3})=\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{\pi}$ $\begin{aligned} & \therefore \frac{\pi}{3}(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{\pi})sec(\frac{\pi}{3})=tan(\frac{\pi}{3})+c \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \sqrt{3}(2)=\sqrt{3}+c \\ \\ & \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow & c=\sqrt{3} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$ On putting the value of $c$ in Eq. (i), we get $\begin{aligned} & xysecx=tanx+\sqrt{3} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow y=\frac{1}{x}(sinx+\sqrt{3}cosx) \\ \\ & y^{'}=\frac{1}{x}(cosx-\sqrt{3}sinx)-\frac{1}{x^{2}}(sinx+\sqrt{3}cosx) \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \text{and}y^{''}=\frac{1}{x}(-sinx-\sqrt{3}cosx)-\frac{1}{x^{2}}(cosx-\sqrt{3}sinx)-\frac{1}{x^{2}}(cosx-\sqrt{3}sinx) \\ & -\frac{2}{x^{3}}(cosx-\sqrt{3}sinx) \\ \\ & \therefore |\frac{\pi}{6}y^{''}(\frac{\pi}{6})+2y^{'}(\frac{\pi}{6})|=|-2|=2 \\ \\ & \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Given, differential equation

$\begin{aligned} & (xcosx)dy+(xysinx+ycosx-1)dx=0,0<x<\frac{\pi}{2} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{xysinx+ycosx-1}{xcosx}=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}+(\frac{xysinx+ycosx}{xcosx})=\frac{1}{xcosx} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}+(tanx+\frac{1}{x})y=\frac{1}{xcosx} \end{aligned}$

Which is linear differential equation in the form of

$\begin{aligned} & \frac{dy}{dx}+Py=Q \\ \\ & \therefore IF=e^{\int (tanx+\frac{1}{x})dx}=e^{(logsecx+logx)}=e^{log(xsecx)}=xsecx \end{aligned}$

$\therefore$ The general solution of the given differential equation

$\begin{aligned} y \cdot IF=\int (Q \times IF)dx+c \\ \\ \Rightarrow y(xsecx)=\int (\frac{1}{xcosx}xsecx)dx+c \\ \\ \Rightarrow xysecx=\int sec^{2}xdx+c \\ \\ \Rightarrow xysecx=tanx+c........(i) \end{aligned}$

Since, $\frac{\pi}{3}y(\frac{\pi}{3})=\sqrt{3} \Rightarrow y(\frac{\pi}{3})=\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{\pi}$

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore \frac{\pi}{3}(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{\pi})sec(\frac{\pi}{3})=tan(\frac{\pi}{3})+c \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \sqrt{3}(2)=\sqrt{3}+c \\ \\ & \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow & c=\sqrt{3} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$

On putting the value of $c$ in Eq. (i), we get

$\begin{aligned} & xysecx=tanx+\sqrt{3} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow y=\frac{1}{x}(sinx+\sqrt{3}cosx) \\ \\ & y^{'}=\frac{1}{x}(cosx-\sqrt{3}sinx)-\frac{1}{x^{2}}(sinx+\sqrt{3}cosx) \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \text{and}y^{''}=\frac{1}{x}(-sinx-\sqrt{3}cosx)-\frac{1}{x^{2}}(cosx-\sqrt{3}sinx)-\frac{1}{x^{2}}(cosx-\sqrt{3}sinx) \\ & -\frac{2}{x^{3}}(cosx-\sqrt{3}sinx) \\ \\ & \therefore |\frac{\pi}{6}y^{''}(\frac{\pi}{6})+2y^{'}(\frac{\pi}{6})|=|-2|=2 \\ \\ & \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_text: D.E. $(1+e^{2x})(\frac{dy}{dx}+y)=1$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}+y=\frac{1}{1+e^{2x}}$ I.F. $=e^{\int 1.dx}=e^{x}$ $\therefore$ Solution $e^{x}y(x)=\int \frac{e^{x}}{1+e^{2x}}dx$ $\Rightarrow e^{x}y(x)=tan^{-1}(e^{x})+C$ $\because$ It passes through $(0,\frac{\pi}{2}),C=\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{\pi}{4}$ $\therefore$ $\underset{x \rightarrow \infty}{lim}e^{x}y(x)=\underset{x \rightarrow \infty}{lim}tan^{-1}(e^{x})+\frac{\pi}{4}$ $=\frac{3\pi}{4}$
questions.explanation_html:
D.E. $(1+e^{2x})(\frac{dy}{dx}+y)=1$

$\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}+y=\frac{1}{1+e^{2x}}$

I.F. $=e^{\int 1.dx}=e^{x}$

$\therefore$ Solution

$e^{x}y(x)=\int \frac{e^{x}}{1+e^{2x}}dx$

$\Rightarrow e^{x}y(x)=tan^{-1}(e^{x})+C$

$\because$ It passes through $(0,\frac{\pi}{2}),C=\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{\pi}{4}$

$\therefore$ $\underset{x \rightarrow \infty}{lim}e^{x}y(x)=\underset{x \rightarrow \infty}{lim}tan^{-1}(e^{x})+\frac{\pi}{4}$

$=\frac{3\pi}{4}$

If $y=y(x),x \in (0,\pi/2)$ be the solution curve of the differential equation

$(sin^{2}2x)\frac{dy}{dx}+(8sin^{2}2x+2sin4x)y=2e^{-4x}(2sin2x+cos2x)$ ,

with $y(\pi/4)=e^{-\pi}$ , then $y(\pi/6)$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $(sin^{2}2x)\frac{dy}{dx}+(8sin^{2}2x+2sin4x)y$ $=2e^{-4x}(2sin2x+cos2x)$ $\frac{dy}{dx}+(8+4cot2x)y=2e^{-4x}(\frac{2sin2x+cos2x}{sin^{2}2x})$ Integrating factor $(I.F.)=e^{\int (8+4cot2x)dx}$ $=e^{8x+2lnsin2x}$ Solution of differential equation $y.e^{8x+2lnsin2x}$ $=\int 2e^{(4x+2lnsin2x)}\frac{(2sin2x+cos2x)}{sin^{2}2x}dx$ $=2\int e^{4x}(2sin2x+cos2x)dx$ $y.e^{8x+2lnsin2x}=e^{4x}sin2x+c$ $y(\frac{\pi}{4})=e^{-\pi}$ $e^{-\pi}.e^{2\pi}=e^{\pi}+c \Rightarrow c=0$ $y(\frac{\pi}{6})=\frac{e^{\frac{2\pi}{3}}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}{e^{(\frac{4\pi}{3}+2ln\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}}$ $=e^{\frac{-2\pi}{3}}.\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$
questions.explanation_html:
$(sin^{2}2x)\frac{dy}{dx}+(8sin^{2}2x+2sin4x)y$

$=2e^{-4x}(2sin2x+cos2x)$

$\frac{dy}{dx}+(8+4cot2x)y=2e^{-4x}(\frac{2sin2x+cos2x}{sin^{2}2x})$

Integrating factor

$(I.F.)=e^{\int (8+4cot2x)dx}$

$=e^{8x+2lnsin2x}$

Solution of differential equation

$y.e^{8x+2lnsin2x}$

$=\int 2e^{(4x+2lnsin2x)}\frac{(2sin2x+cos2x)}{sin^{2}2x}dx$

$=2\int e^{4x}(2sin2x+cos2x)dx$

$y.e^{8x+2lnsin2x}=e^{4x}sin2x+c$

$y(\frac{\pi}{4})=e^{-\pi}$

$e^{-\pi}.e^{2\pi}=e^{\pi}+c \Rightarrow c=0$

$y(\frac{\pi}{6})=\frac{e^{\frac{2\pi}{3}}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}{e^{(\frac{4\pi}{3}+2ln\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}}$

$=e^{\frac{-2\pi}{3}}.\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$

questions.explanation_text: Given, $(1+e^{2x})\frac{dy}{dx}+2(1+y^{2})e^{x}=0$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-2(1+y^{2})e^{x}}{1+e^{2x}}$ $\Rightarrow \int \frac{dy}{1+y^{2}}=\int \frac{-2e^{x}dx}{(1+e^{2x})}$ $\Rightarrow tan^{-1}(y)=\int \frac{-2e^{x}dx}{(1+e^{2x})}$ Now, Let $e^{x}=t$ $\Rightarrow e^{x}dx=dt$ $\Rightarrow tan^{-1}(y)=\int \frac{-2dt}{1+t^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow tan^{-1}(y)=-2tan^{-1}(t)+C$ $\Rightarrow tan^{-1}(y)=-2tan^{-1}(e^{x})+C$ [Putting value of t] Given, y(0) = 0 means when x = 0 the y = 0 $\therefore$ $tan^{-1}(0)=-2tan^{-1}(e^{o})+C$ $\Rightarrow 0=-2 \times \frac{\pi}{4}+C$ $\Rightarrow C=\frac{\pi}{2}$ $\therefore$ $tan^{-1}(y)=2tan^{-1}(e^{x})+\frac{\pi}{2}$ $\Rightarrow y=tan(-2tan^{-1}(e^{x})+\frac{\pi}{2})$ Differentiating both sides, we get $y^{'}=sec^{2}(-2tan^{-1}(e^{x})+\frac{\pi}{2})-2.\frac{e^{x}}{1+e^{2x}}$ $=sec^{2}(-2tan^{-1}(e^{x})+\frac{\pi}{2}) \times \frac{-2e^{x}}{1+e^{2x}}$ $\therefore$ $y^{'}(0)=sec^{2}(-2tan^{-1}(e^{o})+\frac{\pi}{2}) \times \frac{-2e^{o}}{1+e^{o}}$ $=sec^{2}(-2 \times \frac{\pi}{4}+\frac{\pi}{2}) \times \frac{-2}{2}$ $=sec^{2}(0)x-1$ $=1 \times 1$ $=-1$ And $y(log_{e}^{\sqrt{3}})=tan(-2tan^{-1}(e^{log_{e}^{\sqrt{3}}})+\frac{\pi}{2})$ $=tan(-2tan^{-1}(\sqrt{3})+\frac{\pi}{2})$ $=tan(-2 \times \frac{\pi}{3}+\frac{\pi}{2})$ $=tan(-\frac{\pi}{6})$ $=-tan(\frac{\pi}{6})$ $=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ $\therefore$ $6(y^{'}(0)+(y(log_{e}^{\sqrt{3}}))^{2})$ $=6(-1+(\frac{-1}{\sqrt{3}})^{2})$ $=6(-1+\frac{1}{3})=6 \times \frac{-2}{3}=-4$
questions.explanation_html:
Given,

$(1+e^{2x})\frac{dy}{dx}+2(1+y^{2})e^{x}=0$

$\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-2(1+y^{2})e^{x}}{1+e^{2x}}$

$\Rightarrow \int \frac{dy}{1+y^{2}}=\int \frac{-2e^{x}dx}{(1+e^{2x})}$

$\Rightarrow tan^{-1}(y)=\int \frac{-2e^{x}dx}{(1+e^{2x})}$

Now,

Let $e^{x}=t$

$\Rightarrow e^{x}dx=dt$

$\Rightarrow tan^{-1}(y)=\int \frac{-2dt}{1+t^{2}}$

$\Rightarrow tan^{-1}(y)=-2tan^{-1}(t)+C$

$\Rightarrow tan^{-1}(y)=-2tan^{-1}(e^{x})+C$ [Putting value of t]

Given, y(0) = 0 means when x = 0 the y = 0

$\therefore$ $tan^{-1}(0)=-2tan^{-1}(e^{o})+C$

$\Rightarrow 0=-2 \times \frac{\pi}{4}+C$

$\Rightarrow C=\frac{\pi}{2}$

$\therefore$ $tan^{-1}(y)=2tan^{-1}(e^{x})+\frac{\pi}{2}$

$\Rightarrow y=tan(-2tan^{-1}(e^{x})+\frac{\pi}{2})$

Differentiating both sides, we get

$y^{'}=sec^{2}(-2tan^{-1}(e^{x})+\frac{\pi}{2})-2.\frac{e^{x}}{1+e^{2x}}$

$=sec^{2}(-2tan^{-1}(e^{x})+\frac{\pi}{2}) \times \frac{-2e^{x}}{1+e^{2x}}$

$\therefore$ $y^{'}(0)=sec^{2}(-2tan^{-1}(e^{o})+\frac{\pi}{2}) \times \frac{-2e^{o}}{1+e^{o}}$

$=sec^{2}(-2 \times \frac{\pi}{4}+\frac{\pi}{2}) \times \frac{-2}{2}$

$=sec^{2}(0)x-1$

$=1 \times 1$

$=-1$

And

$y(log_{e}^{\sqrt{3}})=tan(-2tan^{-1}(e^{log_{e}^{\sqrt{3}}})+\frac{\pi}{2})$

$=tan(-2tan^{-1}(\sqrt{3})+\frac{\pi}{2})$

$=tan(-2 \times \frac{\pi}{3}+\frac{\pi}{2})$

$=tan(-\frac{\pi}{6})$

$=-tan(\frac{\pi}{6})$

$=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

$\therefore$ $6(y^{'}(0)+(y(log_{e}^{\sqrt{3}}))^{2})$

$=6(-1+(\frac{-1}{\sqrt{3}})^{2})$

$=6(-1+\frac{1}{3})=6 \times \frac{-2}{3}=-4$

questions.question_text: Let $g:(0,\infty) \rightarrow R$ be a differentiable function such that $\int (\frac{x(cosx-sinx)}{e^{x}+1}+\frac{g(x)(e^{x}+1-xe^{x})}{(e^{x}+1)^{2}})dx=\frac{xg(x)}{e^{x}+1}+c$ , for all x > 0, where c is an arbitrary constant. Then :
questions.question_html:
Let $g:(0,\infty) \rightarrow R$ be a differentiable function such that

$\int (\frac{x(cosx-sinx)}{e^{x}+1}+\frac{g(x)(e^{x}+1-xe^{x})}{(e^{x}+1)^{2}})dx=\frac{xg(x)}{e^{x}+1}+c$ , for all x > 0, where c is an arbitrary constant. Then :

options.label: A
options.html: g is decreasing in $(0,\frac{\pi}{4})$

options.label: B
options.html: g' is increasing in $(0,\frac{\pi}{4})$

options.label: C
options.html: g + g' is increasing in $(0,\frac{\pi}{2})$

options.label: D
options.html: g $-$ g' is increasing in $(0,\frac{\pi}{2})$

questions.explanation_text: $\int (\frac{x(cosx-sinx)}{e^{x}+1}+\frac{g(x)(e^{x}+1-xe^{x})}{(e^{x}+1)^{2}})dx=\frac{xg(x)}{e^{x}+1}+c$ On differentiating both sides w.r.t. $x$ , we get $\begin{aligned} & (\frac{x(cosx-sinx)}{e^{x}+1}+\frac{g(x)(e^{x}+1-xe^{x}}{(e^{x}+1)^{2}}) \\ \\ & =\frac{(e^{x}+1)(g(x)+xg^{'}(x))-e^{x} \cdot x \cdot g(x)}{(e^{x}+1)^{2}} \\ \\ & (e^{x}+1)x(cosx-sinx)+g(x)(e^{x}+1-xe^{x}) \\ \\ & =(e^{x}+1)(g(x)+xg^{'}(x))-e^{x} \cdot x \cdot g(x) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow gg^{'}(x)=cosx-sinx \\ \\ & \Rightarrow g(x)=sinx+cosx+C \end{aligned}$ $g(x)$ is increasing in $(0,\pi/4)$ $g''(x)=-sinx-cosx<0$ $\Rightarrow g^{'}(x)$ is decreasing function let $ℎ(x)=g(x)+g^{'}(x)=2cosx+C$ $\Rightarrow h^{'}(x)=g^{'}(x)+g^{''}(x)=-2sinx<0$ $\Rightarrow h$ is decreasing let $\phi(x)=g(x)-g^{'}(x)=2sinx+C$ $\Rightarrow \phi^{'}(x)=g^{'}(x)-g^{''}(x)=2cosx>0$ $\Rightarrow \phi$ is increasing Hence option D is correct.
questions.explanation_html:
$\int (\frac{x(cosx-sinx)}{e^{x}+1}+\frac{g(x)(e^{x}+1-xe^{x})}{(e^{x}+1)^{2}})dx=\frac{xg(x)}{e^{x}+1}+c$

On differentiating both sides w.r.t. $x$ , we get

$\begin{aligned} & (\frac{x(cosx-sinx)}{e^{x}+1}+\frac{g(x)(e^{x}+1-xe^{x}}{(e^{x}+1)^{2}}) \\ \\ & =\frac{(e^{x}+1)(g(x)+xg^{'}(x))-e^{x} \cdot x \cdot g(x)}{(e^{x}+1)^{2}} \\ \\ & (e^{x}+1)x(cosx-sinx)+g(x)(e^{x}+1-xe^{x}) \\ \\ & =(e^{x}+1)(g(x)+xg^{'}(x))-e^{x} \cdot x \cdot g(x) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow gg^{'}(x)=cosx-sinx \\ \\ & \Rightarrow g(x)=sinx+cosx+C \end{aligned}$

$g(x)$ is increasing in $(0,\pi/4)$

$g''(x)=-sinx-cosx<0$

$\Rightarrow g^{'}(x)$ is decreasing function

let $ℎ(x)=g(x)+g^{'}(x)=2cosx+C$

$\Rightarrow h^{'}(x)=g^{'}(x)+g^{''}(x)=-2sinx<0$

$\Rightarrow h$ is decreasing

let $\phi(x)=g(x)-g^{'}(x)=2sinx+C$

$\Rightarrow \phi^{'}(x)=g^{'}(x)-g^{''}(x)=2cosx>0$

$\Rightarrow \phi$ is increasing

Hence option D is correct.

questions.question_text: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution curve of the differential equation $sin(2x^{2})log_{e}(tanx^{2})dy+(4xy-4\sqrt{2}xsin(x^{2}-\frac{\pi}{4}))dx=0$ , $0<x<\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}$ , which passes through the point $(\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{6}},1)$ . Then $|y(\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{3}})|$ is equal to ______________.
questions.question_html:
Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution curve of the differential equation

$sin(2x^{2})log_{e}(tanx^{2})dy+(4xy-4\sqrt{2}xsin(x^{2}-\frac{\pi}{4}))dx=0$ , $0<x<\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}$ , which passes through the point $(\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{6}},1)$ . Then $|y(\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{3}})|$ is equal to ______________.
questions.explanation_text: $\frac{dy}{dx}+y(\frac{4x}{sin(2x^{2})ln(tanx^{2})})=\frac{4\sqrt{2}xsin(x^{2}-\frac{\pi}{4})}{sin(2x^{2})ln(tanx^{2})}$ $I.F=e^{\int \frac{4x}{sin(2x^{2})ln(tanx^{2})}dx}$ $=e^{ln|ln(tanx^{2})}=ln(tanx^{2})$ $\therefore$ $\int d(y.ln(tanx^{2}))=\int \frac{4\sqrt{2}xsin(x^{2}-\frac{\pi}{4})}{sin(2x^{2})}dx$ $\Rightarrow yln(tanx^{2})=ln|\frac{secx^{2}+tanx^{2}}{cosecx^{2}-cotx^{2}}|+C$ $ln(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})=ln(\frac{\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}}}{2-\sqrt{3}})+C$ $e=ln(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})-ln(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2-\sqrt{3}})$ For $y(\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{3}})$ $yln(\sqrt{3})=ln|\frac{2+\sqrt{3}}{\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}|+ln(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})-ln(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{3}})$ $=ln(2+\sqrt{3})+ln(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})+ln(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})-ln(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2-\sqrt{3}})$ $\Rightarrow yln\sqrt{3}=ln(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})$ $\Rightarrow \frac{y}{2}ln3=-\frac{1}{2}ln3$ $\Rightarrow y=1$ $\therefore$ $|y(\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{3}})|=1$ .
questions.explanation_html:
$\frac{dy}{dx}+y(\frac{4x}{sin(2x^{2})ln(tanx^{2})})=\frac{4\sqrt{2}xsin(x^{2}-\frac{\pi}{4})}{sin(2x^{2})ln(tanx^{2})}$

$I.F=e^{\int \frac{4x}{sin(2x^{2})ln(tanx^{2})}dx}$

$=e^{ln|ln(tanx^{2})}=ln(tanx^{2})$

$\therefore$ $\int d(y.ln(tanx^{2}))=\int \frac{4\sqrt{2}xsin(x^{2}-\frac{\pi}{4})}{sin(2x^{2})}dx$

$\Rightarrow yln(tanx^{2})=ln|\frac{secx^{2}+tanx^{2}}{cosecx^{2}-cotx^{2}}|+C$

$ln(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})=ln(\frac{\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}}}{2-\sqrt{3}})+C$

$e=ln(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})-ln(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2-\sqrt{3}})$

For $y(\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{3}})$

$yln(\sqrt{3})=ln|\frac{2+\sqrt{3}}{\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}|+ln(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})-ln(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{3}})$

$=ln(2+\sqrt{3})+ln(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})+ln(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})-ln(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2-\sqrt{3}})$

$\Rightarrow yln\sqrt{3}=ln(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})$

$\Rightarrow \frac{y}{2}ln3=-\frac{1}{2}ln3$

$\Rightarrow y=1$

$\therefore$ $|y(\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{3}})|=1$ .

questions.question_text: Let y = y(x), x > 1, be the solution of the differential equation $(x-1)\frac{dy}{dx}+2xy=\frac{1}{x-1}$ , with $y(2)=\frac{1+e^{4}}{2e^{4}}$ . If $y(3)=\frac{e^{\alpha}+1}{\beta e^{\alpha}}$ , then the value of $\alpha+\beta$ is equal to _________.
questions.question_html: Let y = y(x), x > 1, be the solution of the differential equation $(x-1)\frac{dy}{dx}+2xy=\frac{1}{x-1}$ , with $y(2)=\frac{1+e^{4}}{2e^{4}}$ . If $y(3)=\frac{e^{\alpha}+1}{\beta e^{\alpha}}$ , then the value of $\alpha+\beta$ is equal to _________.
questions.explanation_text: $\frac{dy}{dx}+y(\frac{2x}{x-1})=\frac{1}{(x-1)^{2}}$ $\text{I.F}=e^{\int \frac{2x}{x-1}dx}$ $\begin{aligned} & =e^{2\int (\frac{x-1}{x-1}+\frac{1}{x-1})dx} \\ \\ & =e^{2x+2ln(x-1)} \\ \\ & =e^{2x}(x-1)^{2} \end{aligned}$ $\Rightarrow \int d(y \cdot e^{2x}(x-1)^{2})=\int e^{2x}dx$ $\Rightarrow y \cdot e^{2x}(x-1)^{2}=\frac{e^{2x}}{2}+c$ $↓y(2)=\frac{1+e^{4}}{2e^{4}}$ $\frac{1+e^{4}}{2e^{4}} \cdot e^{4}=\frac{e^{4}}{2}+c$ $\Rightarrow c=\frac{e^{4}}{2}(\frac{1+e^{4}-e^{4}}{e^{4}})=\frac{1}{2}$ $\Rightarrow y \cdot e^{2x}(x-1)^{2}=\frac{e^{2x}+1}{2}$ $↓y(3)=\frac{e^{\alpha}+1}{\beta e^{\alpha}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{e^{\alpha}+1}{\beta e^{\alpha}} \cdot e^{6} \cdot 4=\frac{e^{6}+1}{2}$ $\Rightarrow \alpha=6$ and $\beta=8 \Rightarrow \alpha+\beta=14$
questions.explanation_html:
$\frac{dy}{dx}+y(\frac{2x}{x-1})=\frac{1}{(x-1)^{2}}$

$\text{I.F}=e^{\int \frac{2x}{x-1}dx}$

$\begin{aligned} & =e^{2\int (\frac{x-1}{x-1}+\frac{1}{x-1})dx} \\ \\ & =e^{2x+2ln(x-1)} \\ \\ & =e^{2x}(x-1)^{2} \end{aligned}$

$\Rightarrow \int d(y \cdot e^{2x}(x-1)^{2})=\int e^{2x}dx$

$\Rightarrow y \cdot e^{2x}(x-1)^{2}=\frac{e^{2x}}{2}+c$

$↓y(2)=\frac{1+e^{4}}{2e^{4}}$

$\frac{1+e^{4}}{2e^{4}} \cdot e^{4}=\frac{e^{4}}{2}+c$

$\Rightarrow c=\frac{e^{4}}{2}(\frac{1+e^{4}-e^{4}}{e^{4}})=\frac{1}{2}$

$\Rightarrow y \cdot e^{2x}(x-1)^{2}=\frac{e^{2x}+1}{2}$

$↓y(3)=\frac{e^{\alpha}+1}{\beta e^{\alpha}}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{e^{\alpha}+1}{\beta e^{\alpha}} \cdot e^{6} \cdot 4=\frac{e^{6}+1}{2}$

$\Rightarrow \alpha=6$ and $\beta=8 \Rightarrow \alpha+\beta=14$

questions.question_text: Let $S=(0,2\pi)-{\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3\pi}{4},\frac{3\pi}{2},\frac{7\pi}{4}}$ . Let $y=y(x)$ , x $\in$ S, be the solution curve of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{1+sin2x},y(\frac{\pi}{4})=\frac{1}{2}$ . If the sum of abscissas of all the points of intersection of the curve y = y(x) with the curve $y=\sqrt{2}sinx$ is $\frac{k\pi}{12}$ , then k is equal to _____________.
questions.question_html: Let $S=(0,2\pi)-{\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3\pi}{4},\frac{3\pi}{2},\frac{7\pi}{4}}$ . Let $y=y(x)$ , x $\in$ S, be the solution curve of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{1+sin2x},y(\frac{\pi}{4})=\frac{1}{2}$ . If the sum of abscissas of all the points of intersection of the curve y = y(x) with the curve $y=\sqrt{2}sinx$ is $\frac{k\pi}{12}$ , then k is equal to _____________.
questions.explanation_text: $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{1+sin2x}$ $\Rightarrow dy=\frac{sec^{2}xdx}{(1+tanx)^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow y=-\frac{1}{1+tanx}+c$ When $x=\frac{\pi}{4}$ , $y=\frac{1}{2}$ gives c = 1 So $y=\frac{tanx}{1+tanx} \Rightarrow y=\frac{sinx}{sinx+cosx}$ Now, $y=\sqrt{2}sinx \Rightarrow sinx=0$ or $sinx+cosx=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ $sinx=0$ gives $x=\pi$ only. and $sinx+cosx=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Rightarrow sin(x+\frac{\pi}{4})=\frac{1}{2}$ So $x+\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{5\pi}{6}$ or $\frac{13\pi}{6} \Rightarrow x=\frac{7\pi}{12}$ or $\frac{23\pi}{12}$ Sum of all solutions $=\pi+\frac{7\pi}{12}+\frac{23\pi}{12}=\frac{42\pi}{12}$ Hence, $k=42$ .
questions.explanation_html:
$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{1+sin2x}$

$\Rightarrow dy=\frac{sec^{2}xdx}{(1+tanx)^{2}}$

$\Rightarrow y=-\frac{1}{1+tanx}+c$

When $x=\frac{\pi}{4}$ , $y=\frac{1}{2}$ gives c = 1

So $y=\frac{tanx}{1+tanx} \Rightarrow y=\frac{sinx}{sinx+cosx}$

Now, $y=\sqrt{2}sinx \Rightarrow sinx=0$

or $sinx+cosx=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

$sinx=0$ gives $x=\pi$ only.

and $sinx+cosx=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Rightarrow sin(x+\frac{\pi}{4})=\frac{1}{2}$

So $x+\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{5\pi}{6}$ or $\frac{13\pi}{6} \Rightarrow x=\frac{7\pi}{12}$ or $\frac{23\pi}{12}$

Sum of all solutions $=\pi+\frac{7\pi}{12}+\frac{23\pi}{12}=\frac{42\pi}{12}$

Hence, $k=42$ .

questions.question_text: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution curve of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{1}{x^{2}-1}y=(\frac{x-1}{x+1})^{1/2}$ , $x>1$ passing through the point $(2,\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}})$ . Then $\sqrt{7}y(8)$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution curve of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{1}{x^{2}-1}y=(\frac{x-1}{x+1})^{1/2}$ , $x>1$ passing through the point $(2,\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}})$ . Then $\sqrt{7}y(8)$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{1}{x^{2}-1}y=\sqrt{\frac{x-1}{x+1}},x>1$ Integrating factor I.F. $=e^{\int \frac{1}{x^{2}-1}dx}=e^{\frac{1}{2}ln|\frac{x-1}{x+1}|}$ $=\sqrt{\frac{x-1}{x+1}}$ Solution of differential equation $y\sqrt{\frac{x-1}{x+1}}=\int \frac{x-1}{x+1}dx=\int (1-\frac{2}{x+1})dx$ $y\sqrt{\frac{x-1}{x+1}}=x-2ln|x+1|+C$ Curve passes through $(2,\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}})$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}=2-2ln3+C$ $C=2ln3-\frac{5}{3}$ $y(8) \times \frac{\sqrt{7}}{3}=8-2ln9+2ln3-\frac{5}{3}$ $\sqrt{7}.y(8)=19-6ln3$
questions.explanation_html:
$\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{1}{x^{2}-1}y=\sqrt{\frac{x-1}{x+1}},x>1$

Integrating factor I.F. $=e^{\int \frac{1}{x^{2}-1}dx}=e^{\frac{1}{2}ln|\frac{x-1}{x+1}|}$

$=\sqrt{\frac{x-1}{x+1}}$

Solution of differential equation

$y\sqrt{\frac{x-1}{x+1}}=\int \frac{x-1}{x+1}dx=\int (1-\frac{2}{x+1})dx$

$y\sqrt{\frac{x-1}{x+1}}=x-2ln|x+1|+C$

Curve passes through $(2,\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}})$

$\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}=2-2ln3+C$

$C=2ln3-\frac{5}{3}$

$y(8) \times \frac{\sqrt{7}}{3}=8-2ln9+2ln3-\frac{5}{3}$

$\sqrt{7}.y(8)=19-6ln3$

questions.question_html: Let $y=y_{1}(x)$ and $y=y_{2}(x)$ be two distinct solutions of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}=x+y$ , with $y_{1}(0)=0$ and $y_{2}(0)=1$ respectively. Then, the number of points of intersection of $y=y_{1}(x)$ and $y=y_{2}(x)$ is
questions.explanation_text: $\frac{dy}{dx}=x+y$ Let $x+y=t$ $1+\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dt}{dx}$ $\frac{dt}{dx}-1=t \Rightarrow \int \frac{dt}{t+1}=\int dx$ $ln|t+1|=x+C^{'}$ $|t+1|=Ce^{x}$ $|x+y+1|=Ce^{x}$ For $y_{1}(x),y_{1}(0)=0 \Rightarrow C=1$ For $y_{2}(x),y_{2}(0)=1 \Rightarrow C=2$ $y_{1}(x)$ is given by $|x+y+1|=e^{x}$ $y_{2}(x)$ is given by $|x+y+1|=2e^{x}$ At point of intersection $e^{x}=2e^{x}$ No solution So, there is no point of intersection of $y_{1}(x)$ and $y_{2}(x)$ .
questions.explanation_html:
$\frac{dy}{dx}=x+y$

Let $x+y=t$

$1+\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dt}{dx}$

$\frac{dt}{dx}-1=t \Rightarrow \int \frac{dt}{t+1}=\int dx$

$ln|t+1|=x+C^{'}$

$|t+1|=Ce^{x}$

$|x+y+1|=Ce^{x}$

For $y_{1}(x),y_{1}(0)=0 \Rightarrow C=1$

For $y_{2}(x),y_{2}(0)=1 \Rightarrow C=2$

$y_{1}(x)$ is given by $|x+y+1|=e^{x}$

$y_{2}(x)$ is given by $|x+y+1|=2e^{x}$

At point of intersection

$e^{x}=2e^{x}$

No solution

So, there is no point of intersection of $y_{1}(x)$ and $y_{2}(x)$ .

The slope of the tangent to a curve $C:y=y(x)$ at any point $(x,y)$ on it is $\frac{2e^{2x}-6e^{-x}+9}{2+9e^{-2x}}$ .

If $C$ passes through the points $(0,\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}})$ and $(\alpha,\frac{1}{2}e^{2\alpha})$ , then $e^{\alpha}$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: The slope of the tangent to a curve $C:y=y(x)$ at any point $(x,y)$ on it is $\frac{2e^{2x}-6e^{-x}+9}{2+9e^{-2x}}$ . If $C$ passes through the points $(0,\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}})$ and $(\alpha,\frac{1}{2}e^{2\alpha})$ , then $e^{\alpha}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2e^{2x}-6e^{-x}+9}{2+9e^{-2x}}=e^{2x}-\frac{6e^{-x}}{2+9e^{-2x}}$ $\begin{aligned} & \int dy=\int e^{2x}dx-3\int \underset{\text{put}e^{-x}=t}{\underset{}{1+(\frac{3e^{-x}}{\sqrt{2}})^{2}}}dx \\ \\ & =\frac{e^{2x}}{2}+3\int \frac{dt}{1+(\frac{3t}{\sqrt{2}})^{2}} \\ \\ & =\frac{e^{2x}}{2}+\sqrt{2}tan^{-1}\frac{3t}{\sqrt{2}}+C \end{aligned}$ $y=\frac{e^{2x}}{2}+\sqrt{2}tan^{-1}(\frac{3e^{-x}}{\sqrt{2}})+C$ It is given that the curve passes through $(0,\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}})$ $\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{2}+\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}}=\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{2}tan^{-1}(\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}})+C \end{aligned}$ $\Rightarrow C=\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}}-\sqrt{2}tan^{-1}(\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}})$ Now if $(\alpha,\frac{1}{2}e^{2\alpha})$ satisfies the curve, then $\frac{1}{2}e^{2\alpha}=\frac{e^{2\alpha}}{2}+\sqrt{2}tan^{-1}(\frac{3e^{-\alpha}}{\sqrt{2}})+\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}}-\sqrt{2}tan^{-1}(\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}})$ $tan^{-1}(\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}})-tan^{-1}(\frac{3e^{-\alpha}}{\sqrt{2}})=\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}} \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{\pi}{4}$ $\frac{\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{3e^{-\alpha}}{\sqrt{2}}}{1+\frac{9}{2}e^{-\alpha}}=1$ $\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}e^{\alpha}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}=e^{\alpha}+\frac{9}{2}$ $e^{\alpha}=\frac{\frac{9}{2}+\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}}{\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}-1}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}(\frac{3+\sqrt{2}}{3-\sqrt{2}})$
questions.explanation_html:
$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2e^{2x}-6e^{-x}+9}{2+9e^{-2x}}=e^{2x}-\frac{6e^{-x}}{2+9e^{-2x}}$

$\begin{aligned} & \int dy=\int e^{2x}dx-3\int \underset{\text{put}e^{-x}=t}{\underset{}{1+(\frac{3e^{-x}}{\sqrt{2}})^{2}}}dx \\ \\ & =\frac{e^{2x}}{2}+3\int \frac{dt}{1+(\frac{3t}{\sqrt{2}})^{2}} \\ \\ & =\frac{e^{2x}}{2}+\sqrt{2}tan^{-1}\frac{3t}{\sqrt{2}}+C \end{aligned}$

$y=\frac{e^{2x}}{2}+\sqrt{2}tan^{-1}(\frac{3e^{-x}}{\sqrt{2}})+C$

It is given that the curve passes through

$(0,\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}})$

$\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{2}+\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}}=\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{2}tan^{-1}(\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}})+C \end{aligned}$

$\Rightarrow C=\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}}-\sqrt{2}tan^{-1}(\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}})$

Now if $(\alpha,\frac{1}{2}e^{2\alpha})$ satisfies the curve, then

$\frac{1}{2}e^{2\alpha}=\frac{e^{2\alpha}}{2}+\sqrt{2}tan^{-1}(\frac{3e^{-\alpha}}{\sqrt{2}})+\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}}-\sqrt{2}tan^{-1}(\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}})$

$tan^{-1}(\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}})-tan^{-1}(\frac{3e^{-\alpha}}{\sqrt{2}})=\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}} \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{\pi}{4}$

$\frac{\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{3e^{-\alpha}}{\sqrt{2}}}{1+\frac{9}{2}e^{-\alpha}}=1$

$\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}e^{\alpha}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}=e^{\alpha}+\frac{9}{2}$

$e^{\alpha}=\frac{\frac{9}{2}+\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}}{\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}-1}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}(\frac{3+\sqrt{2}}{3-\sqrt{2}})$

questions.question_html:
Let the solution curve of the differential equation

$x\frac{dy}{dx}-y=\sqrt{y^{2}+16x^{2}}$ , $y(1)=3$ be $y=y(x)$ . Then y(2) is equal to:
questions.explanation_text: Given, $x\frac{dy}{dx}-y=\sqrt{y^{2}+16x}$ $\Rightarrow x\frac{dy}{dx}=y+\sqrt{y^{2}+16x}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y}{x}+\sqrt{(\frac{y}{x})^{2}+16}$ This is a homogenous different equation. Let $\frac{y}{x}=v$ $\Rightarrow y=vx$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=v+x\frac{dv}{dx}$ $\therefore$ $v+x\frac{dv}{dx}=v+\sqrt{v^{2}+16}$ $\Rightarrow$ $x\frac{dv}{dx}=\sqrt{v^{2}+16}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dv}{\sqrt{v^{2}+16}}=\frac{dx}{x}$ Integrating both sides, we get $\int \frac{dv}{\sqrt{v^{2}+16}}=\int \frac{dx}{x}$ $\Rightarrow ln|v+\sqrt{v^{2}+16}|=lnx+lnc$ $\Rightarrow v+\sqrt{v^{2}+16}=cx$ Now putting, $v=\frac{y}{x}$ , we get $\frac{y}{x}+\sqrt{\frac{y^{2}}{x^{2}}+16}=cx$ $\Rightarrow \frac{y}{x}+\sqrt{\frac{y^{2}+16x^{2}}{x^{2}}}=cx$ $\Rightarrow y+\sqrt{y^{2}+16x^{2}}=cx^{2}$ ...... (1) Given, $y(1)=3$ $\therefore$ When x = 1 then y = 3. Putting in equation (1) we get, $3+\sqrt{9+16}=c.1$ $\Rightarrow c=8$ $\therefore$ Solution of equation, $y+\sqrt{y^{2}+16x^{2}}=8x^{2}$ Now, y(2) means when x = 2 then y = ? $\therefore$ $y+\sqrt{y^{2}+16 \times 4}=8 \times 4$ $\Rightarrow y=15$
questions.explanation_html:
Given,

$x\frac{dy}{dx}-y=\sqrt{y^{2}+16x}$

$\Rightarrow x\frac{dy}{dx}=y+\sqrt{y^{2}+16x}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y}{x}+\sqrt{(\frac{y}{x})^{2}+16}$

This is a homogenous different equation.

Let $\frac{y}{x}=v$

$\Rightarrow y=vx$

$\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=v+x\frac{dv}{dx}$

$\therefore$ $v+x\frac{dv}{dx}=v+\sqrt{v^{2}+16}$

$\Rightarrow$ $x\frac{dv}{dx}=\sqrt{v^{2}+16}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{dv}{\sqrt{v^{2}+16}}=\frac{dx}{x}$

Integrating both sides, we get

$\int \frac{dv}{\sqrt{v^{2}+16}}=\int \frac{dx}{x}$

$\Rightarrow ln|v+\sqrt{v^{2}+16}|=lnx+lnc$

$\Rightarrow v+\sqrt{v^{2}+16}=cx$

Now putting, $v=\frac{y}{x}$ , we get

$\frac{y}{x}+\sqrt{\frac{y^{2}}{x^{2}}+16}=cx$

$\Rightarrow \frac{y}{x}+\sqrt{\frac{y^{2}+16x^{2}}{x^{2}}}=cx$

$\Rightarrow y+\sqrt{y^{2}+16x^{2}}=cx^{2}$ ...... (1)

Given, $y(1)=3$

$\therefore$ When x = 1 then y = 3.

Putting in equation (1) we get,

$3+\sqrt{9+16}=c.1$

$\Rightarrow c=8$

$\therefore$ Solution of equation,

$y+\sqrt{y^{2}+16x^{2}}=8x^{2}$

Now, y(2) means when x = 2 then y = ?

$\therefore$ $y+\sqrt{y^{2}+16 \times 4}=8 \times 4$

$\Rightarrow y=15$

questions.explanation_text: $\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{y(3x^{2}-1)}{x(1-x^{2})}=\frac{4x^{3}}{x(1-x^{2})}$ $IF=e^{\int \frac{3x^{2}-1}{x-x^{3}}dx}=e^{-ln|x^{3}-x|}=e^{-ln(x^{3}-x)}=\frac{1}{x^{3}-x}$ Solution of D.E. can be given by $y.\frac{1}{x^{3}-x}=\int \frac{4x^{3}}{x(1-x^{2})}.\frac{1}{x(x^{2}-1)}dx$ $\Rightarrow \frac{y}{x^{3}-x}=\int \frac{-4x}{(x^{2}-1)^{2}}dx$ $\Rightarrow \frac{y}{x^{3}-x}=\frac{2}{(x^{2}-1)}+c$ at x = 2, y = $-$ 2 $\frac{-2}{6}=\frac{2}{3}+c \Rightarrow c=-1$ at $x=3 \Rightarrow \frac{y}{24}=\frac{2}{8}-1 \Rightarrow y=-18$
questions.explanation_html:
$\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{y(3x^{2}-1)}{x(1-x^{2})}=\frac{4x^{3}}{x(1-x^{2})}$

$IF=e^{\int \frac{3x^{2}-1}{x-x^{3}}dx}=e^{-ln|x^{3}-x|}=e^{-ln(x^{3}-x)}=\frac{1}{x^{3}-x}$

Solution of D.E. can be given by

$y.\frac{1}{x^{3}-x}=\int \frac{4x^{3}}{x(1-x^{2})}.\frac{1}{x(x^{2}-1)}dx$

at x = 2, y = $-$ 2

at $x=3 \Rightarrow \frac{y}{24}=\frac{2}{8}-1 \Rightarrow y=-18$

questions.question_text: If $y=y(x)$ is the solution of the differential equation $x\frac{dy}{dx}+2y=xe^{x}$ , $y(1)=0$ then the local maximum value of the function $z(x)=x^{2}y(x)-e^{x},x \in R$ is :
questions.question_html:
If $y=y(x)$ is the solution of the differential equation

$x\frac{dy}{dx}+2y=xe^{x}$ , $y(1)=0$ then the local maximum value

of the function $z(x)=x^{2}y(x)-e^{x},x \in R$ is :
questions.explanation_text: $x\frac{dy}{dx}+2y=xe^{x},y(1)=0$ $\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{2}{x}y=e^{x}$ , then $e^{\int \frac{2}{x}dx}dx=x^{2}$ $y.x^{2}=\int x^{2}e^{x}dx$ $yx^{2}=x^{2}e^{x}-\int 2xe^{x}dx$ $=x^{2}e^{x}-2(xe^{x}-e^{x})+c$ $yx^{2}=x^{2}e^{x}-2xe^{x}+2e^{x}+c$ $yx^{2}=(x^{2}-2x+2)e^{x}+c$ $0=e+c \Rightarrow c=-e$ $y(x).x^{2}-e^{x}=(x-1)^{2}e^{x}-e$ $z(x)=(x-1)^{2}e^{x}-e$ For local maximum $z^{'}(x)=0$ $\therefore$ $2(x-1)e^{x}+(x-1)^{2}e^{x}=0$ $\therefore$ $x=-1$ And local maximum value $=z(-1)$ $=\frac{4}{e}-e$
questions.explanation_html:
$x\frac{dy}{dx}+2y=xe^{x},y(1)=0$

$\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{2}{x}y=e^{x}$ , then $e^{\int \frac{2}{x}dx}dx=x^{2}$

$y.x^{2}=\int x^{2}e^{x}dx$

$yx^{2}=x^{2}e^{x}-\int 2xe^{x}dx$

$=x^{2}e^{x}-2(xe^{x}-e^{x})+c$

$yx^{2}=x^{2}e^{x}-2xe^{x}+2e^{x}+c$

$yx^{2}=(x^{2}-2x+2)e^{x}+c$

$0=e+c \Rightarrow c=-e$

$y(x).x^{2}-e^{x}=(x-1)^{2}e^{x}-e$

$z(x)=(x-1)^{2}e^{x}-e$

For local maximum $z^{'}(x)=0$

$\therefore$ $2(x-1)e^{x}+(x-1)^{2}e^{x}=0$

$\therefore$ $x=-1$

And local maximum value $=z(-1)$

$=\frac{4}{e}-e$

questions.explanation_html:
$(x+1)\frac{dy}{dx}-y=e^{3x}(x+1)^{2}$

$\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{y}{x+1}=e^{3x}(x+1)$

If $e^{-\int \frac{1}{x+1}x}=e^{-log(x+1)}=\frac{1}{x+1}$

$\therefore$ $y(\frac{1}{x+1})=\int \frac{e^{3x}(x+1)}{x+1}dx$

$\frac{y}{x+1}=\int e^{3x}dx$

$\frac{y}{x+1}=\frac{e^{3x}}{3}+c$

$\because$ $y(0)=\frac{1}{3}$

$\frac{1}{3}=\frac{1}{3}+c$

$\therefore$ $c=0$

So : $y=\frac{e^{3x}}{3}(x+1)$

$y^{'}=e^{3x}(x+1)+\frac{e^{3x}}{3}=e^{3x}(x+\frac{4}{3})$

$y^{''}=3e^{3x}(x+\frac{4}{3})+e^{3x}=e^{3x}(3x+5)$

$y^{'}=0$ at $x=\frac{-4}{3}$ & $y^{''}=e^{-4}(1)>0$ at $x=\frac{-4}{3}$

$\Rightarrow x=\frac{-4}{3}$ is point of local minima

If $a$ and $b$ are respectively the $x$ - and $y$ -intercepts of the tangent to the curve at $x=0$ , then the value of $a-4b$ is equal to _____________.
questions.question_html: Suppose $y=y(x)$ be the solution curve to the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}-y=2-e^{-x}$ such that $\underset{x \rightarrow \infty}{lim}y(x)$ is finite. If $a$ and $b$ are respectively the $x$ - and $y$ -intercepts of the tangent to the curve at $x=0$ , then the value of $a-4b$ is equal to _____________.
questions.explanation_text: IF $=e^{-x}$ $y.e^{-x}=-2e^{-x}+\frac{e^{-2x}}{2}+C$ $\Rightarrow y=-2+e^{-x}+Ce^{x}$ $\underset{x \rightarrow \infty}{lim}y(x)$ is finite so $C=0$ $y=-2+e^{-x}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=-e^{-x} \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}|_{x=0}=-1$ Equation of tangent $y+1=-1(x-0)$ or $y+x=-1$ So $a=-1,b=-1$ $\Rightarrow a-4b=3$

IF $=e^{-x}$

$y.e^{-x}=-2e^{-x}+\frac{e^{-2x}}{2}+C$

$\Rightarrow y=-2+e^{-x}+Ce^{x}$

$\underset{x \rightarrow \infty}{lim}y(x)$ is finite so $C=0$

$y=-2+e^{-x}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=-e^{-x} \Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}|_{x=0}=-1$

Equation of tangent

$y+1=-1(x-0)$

or $y+x=-1$

So $a=-1,b=-1$

$\Rightarrow a-4b=3$

If $y(\frac{\pi}{3})=\frac{\pi^{2}}{18}e^{-tan^{-1}(\alpha)}$ , then the value of 3 $\alpha$ 2 is equal to ___________.
questions.question_html: Let y = y(x) be the solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{\sqrt{2}y}{2cos^{4}x-cos^{2}x}=xe^{tan^{-1}(\sqrt{2}cot2x)},0<x<\frac{\pi}{2}$ with $y(\frac{\pi}{4})=\frac{\pi^{2}}{32}$ . If $y(\frac{\pi}{3})=\frac{\pi^{2}}{18}e^{-tan^{-1}(\alpha)}$ , then the value of 3 $\alpha$ 2 is equal to ___________.
questions.explanation_text: $\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{2\sqrt{2}y}{1+cos^{2}2x}=xe^{tan^{-1}(\sqrt{2}cot2x)}$ I.F. $=e^{\int \frac{2\sqrt{2}dx}{1+cos^{2}2x}}=e^{\sqrt{2}\int \frac{2sec^{2}2x}{2+tan^{2}2x}dx}$ $=e^{tan^{-1}(\frac{tan2x}{\sqrt{2}})}$ $\Rightarrow y \cdot e^{tan^{-1}(\frac{tan2x}{\sqrt{2}})}=\int xe^{tan^{-1}(\sqrt{2}cot2x)}$ $\cdot e^{tan^{-1}(\frac{tan2x}{\sqrt{2}})}dx+c$ $\Rightarrow y \cdot e^{tan^{-1}(\frac{tan2x}{\sqrt{2}})}=e^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \cdot \frac{x^{2}}{2}+c$ When $x=\frac{\pi}{4},y=\frac{\pi^{2}}{32}$ gives $c=0$ When $x=\frac{\pi}{3},y=\frac{\pi^{2}}{18}e^{-tan^{-1}\alpha}$ So $\frac{\pi^{2}}{18}e^{-tan^{-1}\alpha} \cdot e^{-tan^{-1}(-\sqrt{\frac{3}{2})}}=e^{\pi/2}\frac{\pi^{2}}{18}$ $\Rightarrow -tan^{-1}\alpha+tan^{-1}(\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}})=\frac{\pi}{2}$ $\Rightarrow tan^{-1}(-\alpha)=tan^{-1}(\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}})$ $\Rightarrow \alpha=-\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \Rightarrow 3\alpha^{2}=2$
questions.explanation_html:
$\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{2\sqrt{2}y}{1+cos^{2}2x}=xe^{tan^{-1}(\sqrt{2}cot2x)}$

I.F. $=e^{\int \frac{2\sqrt{2}dx}{1+cos^{2}2x}}=e^{\sqrt{2}\int \frac{2sec^{2}2x}{2+tan^{2}2x}dx}$ $=e^{tan^{-1}(\frac{tan2x}{\sqrt{2}})}$

$\Rightarrow y \cdot e^{tan^{-1}(\frac{tan2x}{\sqrt{2}})}=\int xe^{tan^{-1}(\sqrt{2}cot2x)}$

$\cdot e^{tan^{-1}(\frac{tan2x}{\sqrt{2}})}dx+c$

$\Rightarrow y \cdot e^{tan^{-1}(\frac{tan2x}{\sqrt{2}})}=e^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \cdot \frac{x^{2}}{2}+c$

When $x=\frac{\pi}{4},y=\frac{\pi^{2}}{32}$ gives $c=0$

When $x=\frac{\pi}{3},y=\frac{\pi^{2}}{18}e^{-tan^{-1}\alpha}$

So $\frac{\pi^{2}}{18}e^{-tan^{-1}\alpha} \cdot e^{-tan^{-1}(-\sqrt{\frac{3}{2})}}=e^{\pi/2}\frac{\pi^{2}}{18}$

$\Rightarrow -tan^{-1}\alpha+tan^{-1}(\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}})=\frac{\pi}{2}$

$\Rightarrow tan^{-1}(-\alpha)=tan^{-1}(\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}})$

$\Rightarrow \alpha=-\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \Rightarrow 3\alpha^{2}=2$

questions.question_html: If the solution curve of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x+y-2}{x-y}$ passes through the points $(2,1)$ and $(k+1,2),k>0$ , then
questions.explanation_text: $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x+y-2}{x-y}=\frac{(x-1)+(y-1)}{(x-1)-(y-1)}$ Let $x-1=X,y-1=Y$ $\frac{dY}{dX}=\frac{X+Y}{X-Y}$ Let $Y=tX \Rightarrow \frac{dY}{dX}=t+X\frac{dt}{dX}$ $t+X\frac{dt}{dX}=\frac{1+t}{1-t}$ $X\frac{dt}{dX}=\frac{1+t}{1-t}-t=\frac{1+t^{2}}{1-t}$ $\int \frac{1-t}{1+t^{2}}dt=\int \frac{dX}{X}$ $\begin{aligned} & tan^{-1}t-\frac{1}{2}ln(1+t^{2})=ln|X|+c \\ \\ & tan^{-1}(\frac{y-1}{x-1})-\frac{1}{2}ln(1+(\frac{y-1}{x-1})^{2})=ln|x-1|+c \end{aligned}$ Curve passes through $(2,1)$ $0-0=0+c \Rightarrow c=0$ If $(k+1,2)$ also satisfies the curve $\begin{aligned} & tan^{-1}(\frac{1}{k})-\frac{1}{2}ln(\frac{1+k^{2}}{k^{2}})=lnk \\ \\ & 2tan^{-1}(\frac{1}{k})=ln(1+k^{2}) \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x+y-2}{x-y}=\frac{(x-1)+(y-1)}{(x-1)-(y-1)}$

Let $x-1=X,y-1=Y$

$\frac{dY}{dX}=\frac{X+Y}{X-Y}$

Let $Y=tX \Rightarrow \frac{dY}{dX}=t+X\frac{dt}{dX}$

$t+X\frac{dt}{dX}=\frac{1+t}{1-t}$

$X\frac{dt}{dX}=\frac{1+t}{1-t}-t=\frac{1+t^{2}}{1-t}$

$\int \frac{1-t}{1+t^{2}}dt=\int \frac{dX}{X}$

$\begin{aligned} & tan^{-1}t-\frac{1}{2}ln(1+t^{2})=ln|X|+c \\ \\ & tan^{-1}(\frac{y-1}{x-1})-\frac{1}{2}ln(1+(\frac{y-1}{x-1})^{2})=ln|x-1|+c \end{aligned}$

Curve passes through $(2,1)$

$0-0=0+c \Rightarrow c=0$

If $(k+1,2)$ also satisfies the curve

$\begin{aligned} & tan^{-1}(\frac{1}{k})-\frac{1}{2}ln(\frac{1+k^{2}}{k^{2}})=lnk \\ \\ & 2tan^{-1}(\frac{1}{k})=ln(1+k^{2}) \end{aligned}$

Integrating factor $(I.F.)=e^{\int \frac{x}{x^{2}-1}dx}$ $=e^{\frac{1}{2}ln|x^{2}-1|}=\sqrt{|x^{2}-1|}$ $=\sqrt{1-x^{2}}$ $\because$ $x \in (-1,1)$ Solution of differential equation $y\sqrt{1-x^{2}}=\int (x^{4}+2x)dx=\frac{x^{5}}{5}+x^{2}+c$ Curve is passing through origin, $c=0$ $y=\frac{x^{5}+5x^{2}}{5\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$ $\int_{\frac{-\sqrt{3}}{2}}^{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}\frac{x^{5}+5x^{2}}{5\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}dx=0+2\int_{0}^{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}\frac{x^{2}}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}dx$ put $x=sin\theta$ $dx=cos\theta d\theta$ $I=2\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\frac{sin^{2}\theta.cos\theta d\theta}{cos\theta}$ $=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}(1-cos2\theta)d\theta$ $=(\theta-\frac{sin2\theta}{2})|_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}$ $=\frac{\pi}{3}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{xy}{x^{2}-1}=\frac{x^{4}+2x}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$

which is first order linear differential equation.

Integrating factor $(I.F.)=e^{\int \frac{x}{x^{2}-1}dx}$

$=e^{\frac{1}{2}ln|x^{2}-1|}=\sqrt{|x^{2}-1|}$

$=\sqrt{1-x^{2}}$

$\because$ $x \in (-1,1)$

Solution of differential equation

$y\sqrt{1-x^{2}}=\int (x^{4}+2x)dx=\frac{x^{5}}{5}+x^{2}+c$

Curve is passing through origin, $c=0$

$y=\frac{x^{5}+5x^{2}}{5\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$

$\int_{\frac{-\sqrt{3}}{2}}^{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}\frac{x^{5}+5x^{2}}{5\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}dx=0+2\int_{0}^{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}\frac{x^{2}}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}dx$

put $x=sin\theta$

$dx=cos\theta d\theta$

$I=2\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\frac{sin^{2}\theta.cos\theta d\theta}{cos\theta}$

$=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}(1-cos2\theta)d\theta$

$=(\theta-\frac{sin2\theta}{2})|_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}$

$=\frac{\pi}{3}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$

questions.question_html: The general solution of the differential equation $(x-y^{2})dx+y(5x+y^{2})dy=0$ is :
questions.explanation_text: $(x-y^{2})dx+y(5x+y^{2})dy=0$ $y\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y^{2}-x}{5x+y^{2}}$ Let $y^{2}=t$ $\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{dt}{dx}=\frac{t-x}{5x+t}$ Now substitute, $t=vx$ $\begin{aligned} & \frac{dt}{dx}=v+x\frac{dv}{dx} \\ \\ & \frac{1}{2}{v+x\frac{dv}{dx}}=\frac{v-1}{5+v} \\ \\ & x\frac{dv}{dx}=\frac{2v-2}{5+v}-v=\frac{-3v-v^{2}-2}{5+v} \\ \\ & \int \frac{5+v}{v^{2}+3v+2}dv=\int -\frac{dx}{x} \\ \\ & \int \frac{4}{v+1}dv-\int \frac{3}{v+2}dv=-\int \frac{dx}{x} \\ \\ & 4ln|v+1|-3ln|v+2|=-lnx+lnC \\ \\ & |\frac{(v+1)^{4}}{(v+2)^{3}}|=\frac{c}{x} \\ \\ & |\frac{(\frac{y^{2}}{x}+1)^{4}}{(\frac{y^{2}}{x}+2)^{3}}|=\frac{c}{x} \\ \\ & |(y^{2}+x)^{4}|=C|(y^{2}+2x)^{3}| \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
$(x-y^{2})dx+y(5x+y^{2})dy=0$

$y\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y^{2}-x}{5x+y^{2}}$

Let $y^{2}=t$ $\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{dt}{dx}=\frac{t-x}{5x+t}$

Now substitute, $t=vx$

$\begin{aligned} & \frac{dt}{dx}=v+x\frac{dv}{dx} \\ \\ & \frac{1}{2}{v+x\frac{dv}{dx}}=\frac{v-1}{5+v} \\ \\ & x\frac{dv}{dx}=\frac{2v-2}{5+v}-v=\frac{-3v-v^{2}-2}{5+v} \\ \\ & \int \frac{5+v}{v^{2}+3v+2}dv=\int -\frac{dx}{x} \\ \\ & \int \frac{4}{v+1}dv-\int \frac{3}{v+2}dv=-\int \frac{dx}{x} \\ \\ & 4ln|v+1|-3ln|v+2|=-lnx+lnC \\ \\ & |\frac{(v+1)^{4}}{(v+2)^{3}}|=\frac{c}{x} \\ \\ & |\frac{(\frac{y^{2}}{x}+1)^{4}}{(\frac{y^{2}}{x}+2)^{3}}|=\frac{c}{x} \\ \\ & |(y^{2}+x)^{4}|=C|(y^{2}+2x)^{3}| \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_text: Given differential equation $2ye^{\frac{x}{y^{2}}}dx+(y^{2}-4xe^{\frac{x}{y^{2}}})dy=0,x(1)=0$ $\Rightarrow e^{\frac{x}{y^{2}}}[2ydx-4xdy]=-y^{2}dy$ $\Rightarrow e^{\frac{x}{y^{2}}}[\frac{2y^{2}dx-4xydy}{y^{4}}]=\frac{-1}{y}dy$ $\Rightarrow 2e^{\frac{x}{y^{2}}}d(\frac{x}{y^{2}})=-\frac{1}{y}dy$ $\Rightarrow 2e^{\frac{x}{y^{2}}}=-lny+c$ ...... (i) Now, using x(1) = 0, c = 2 So, for x(e), Put y = e in (i) $2e^{\frac{x}{e^{2}}}=-1+2$ $\Rightarrow \frac{x}{e^{2}}=ln(\frac{1}{2}) \Rightarrow x(e)=-e^{2}ln2$
questions.explanation_html:
Given differential equation

$2ye^{\frac{x}{y^{2}}}dx+(y^{2}-4xe^{\frac{x}{y^{2}}})dy=0,x(1)=0$

$\Rightarrow e^{\frac{x}{y^{2}}}[2ydx-4xdy]=-y^{2}dy$

Now, using x(1) = 0, c = 2

So, for x(e), Put y = e in (i)

$2e^{\frac{x}{e^{2}}}=-1+2$

$\Rightarrow \frac{x}{e^{2}}=ln(\frac{1}{2}) \Rightarrow x(e)=-e^{2}ln2$

questions.question_text: If the solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}+e^{x}(x^{2}-2)y=(x^{2}-2x)(x^{2}-2)e^{2x}$ satisfies $y(0)=0$ , then the value of y(2) is _______________.
questions.question_html:
If the solution of the differential equation

$\frac{dy}{dx}+e^{x}(x^{2}-2)y=(x^{2}-2x)(x^{2}-2)e^{2x}$ satisfies $y(0)=0$ , then the value of y(2) is _______________.
questions.explanation_html:
$\because$ $\frac{dy}{dx}+e^{x}(x^{2}-2)y=(x^{2}-2x)(x^{2}-2)e^{2x}$

Here, $I.F.=e^{\int e^{x}(x^{2}-2)dx}$

$=e^{(x^{2}-2x)e^{x}}$

$\therefore$ Solution of the differential equation is

$y.e^{(x^{2}-2x)e^{x}}=\int (x^{2}-2x)(x^{2}-2)e^{2x}.e^{(x^{2}-2x)e^{x}}dx$

$=\int (x^{2}-2x)e^{x}.(x^{2}-2)e^{x}.e^{(x^{2}-2x)e^{x}}dx$

Let $(x^{2}-2x)e^{x}=t$

$\therefore$ $(x^{2}-2)e^{x}dx=dt$

$y.e^{(x^{2}-2x)e^{x}}=\int t.e^{t}dt$

$y.e^{(x^{2}-2x)e^{x}}=(x^{2}-2x-1)e^{(x^{2}-2x)e^{x}}+c$

$\therefore$ $y(0)=0$

$\therefore$ $c=1$

$\therefore$ $y=(x^{2}-2x-1)+e^{(2x-x^{2})e^{x}}$

$\therefore$ $y(2)=-1+1=0$

questions.question_text: If the solution curve $y=y(x)$ of the differential equation $y^{2}dx+(x^{2}-xy+y^{2})dy=0$ , which passes through the point (1, 1) and intersects the line $y=\sqrt{3}x$ at the point $(\alpha,\sqrt{3}\alpha)$ , then value of $log_{e}(\sqrt{3}\alpha)$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: If the solution curve $y=y(x)$ of the differential equation $y^{2}dx+(x^{2}-xy+y^{2})dy=0$ , which passes through the point (1, 1) and intersects the line $y=\sqrt{3}x$ at the point $(\alpha,\sqrt{3}\alpha)$ , then value of $log_{e}(\sqrt{3}\alpha)$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y^{2}}{xy-x^{2}-y^{2}}$ Put $y=vx$ we get $v+x\frac{dv}{dx}=\frac{v^{2}}{v-1-v^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow x\frac{dv}{dx}=\frac{v^{2}-v^{2}+v+v^{3}}{v-1-v^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow \int \frac{v-1-v^{2}}{v(1+v^{2})}dv=\int \frac{dx}{x}$ $tan^{-1}(\frac{y}{x})-ln(\frac{y}{x})=lnx+c$ As it passes through (1, 1) $c=\frac{\pi}{4}$ $\Rightarrow tan^{-1}(\frac{y}{x})ln(\frac{y}{x})=lnx+\frac{\pi}{4}$ Put $y=\sqrt{3}x$ we get $\Rightarrow \frac{\pi}{3}-ln\sqrt{3}=lnx+\frac{\pi}{4}$ $\Rightarrow lnx=\frac{\pi}{12}-ln\sqrt{3}=ln\alpha$ $\therefore$ $ln(\sqrt{3}\alpha)=ln\sqrt{3}+ln\alpha$ $=ln\sqrt{3}+\frac{\pi}{12}-ln\sqrt{3}=\frac{\pi}{12}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y^{2}}{xy-x^{2}-y^{2}}$

Put $y=vx$ we get

$v+x\frac{dv}{dx}=\frac{v^{2}}{v-1-v^{2}}$

$\Rightarrow x\frac{dv}{dx}=\frac{v^{2}-v^{2}+v+v^{3}}{v-1-v^{2}}$

$\Rightarrow \int \frac{v-1-v^{2}}{v(1+v^{2})}dv=\int \frac{dx}{x}$

$tan^{-1}(\frac{y}{x})-ln(\frac{y}{x})=lnx+c$

As it passes through (1, 1)

$c=\frac{\pi}{4}$

$\Rightarrow tan^{-1}(\frac{y}{x})ln(\frac{y}{x})=lnx+\frac{\pi}{4}$

Put $y=\sqrt{3}x$ we get

$\Rightarrow \frac{\pi}{3}-ln\sqrt{3}=lnx+\frac{\pi}{4}$

$\Rightarrow lnx=\frac{\pi}{12}-ln\sqrt{3}=ln\alpha$

$\therefore$ $ln(\sqrt{3}\alpha)=ln\sqrt{3}+ln\alpha$

$=ln\sqrt{3}+\frac{\pi}{12}-ln\sqrt{3}=\frac{\pi}{12}$

questions.question_text: Let a curve $y=y(x)$ pass through the point $(3,3)$ and the area of the region under this curve, above the $x$ -axis and between the abscissae 3 and $x(>3)$ be $(\frac{y}{x})^{3}$ . If this curve also passes through the point $(\alpha,6\sqrt{10})$ in the first quadrant, then $\alpha$ is equal to ___________.
questions.question_html: Let a curve $y=y(x)$ pass through the point $(3,3)$ and the area of the region under this curve, above the $x$ -axis and between the abscissae 3 and $x(>3)$ be $(\frac{y}{x})^{3}$ . If this curve also passes through the point $(\alpha,6\sqrt{10})$ in the first quadrant, then $\alpha$ is equal to ___________.
questions.explanation_text: $\int_{3}^{x}f(x)dx=(\frac{f(x)}{x})^{3}$ $x^{3}.\int_{3}^{x}f(x)dx=f^{3}(x)$ Differentiate w.r.t. x $x^{3}f(x)+3x^{2}.\frac{f^{3}(x)}{x^{3}}=3f^{2}(x)f^{'}(x)$ $\Rightarrow 3y^{2}\frac{dy}{dx}=x^{3}y+\frac{3y^{3}}{x}$ $3xy\frac{dy}{dx}=x^{4}+3y^{2}$ Let $y^{2}=t$ $\frac{3}{2}\frac{dt}{dx}=x^{3}+\frac{3t}{x}$ $\frac{dt}{dx}-\frac{2t}{x}=\frac{2x^{3}}{3}$ $I.F.=.e^{\int -\frac{2}{x}dx}=\frac{1}{x^{2}}$ Solution of differential equation $t.\frac{1}{x^{2}}=\int \frac{2}{3}xdx$ $\frac{y^{2}}{x^{2}}=\frac{x^{2}}{3}+C$ $y^{2}=\frac{x^{4}}{3}+Cx^{2}$ Curve passes through $(3,3) \Rightarrow C=-2$ $y^{2}=\frac{x^{4}}{3}-2x^{2}$ Which passes through $(\alpha,6\sqrt{10})$ $\frac{\alpha^{4}-6\alpha^{2}}{3}=360$ $\alpha^{4}-6\alpha^{2}-1080=0$ $\alpha=6$
questions.explanation_html:
$\int_{3}^{x}f(x)dx=(\frac{f(x)}{x})^{3}$

$x^{3}.\int_{3}^{x}f(x)dx=f^{3}(x)$

Differentiate w.r.t. x

$x^{3}f(x)+3x^{2}.\frac{f^{3}(x)}{x^{3}}=3f^{2}(x)f^{'}(x)$

$\Rightarrow 3y^{2}\frac{dy}{dx}=x^{3}y+\frac{3y^{3}}{x}$

$3xy\frac{dy}{dx}=x^{4}+3y^{2}$

Let $y^{2}=t$

$\frac{3}{2}\frac{dt}{dx}=x^{3}+\frac{3t}{x}$

$\frac{dt}{dx}-\frac{2t}{x}=\frac{2x^{3}}{3}$

$I.F.=.e^{\int -\frac{2}{x}dx}=\frac{1}{x^{2}}$

Solution of differential equation

$t.\frac{1}{x^{2}}=\int \frac{2}{3}xdx$

$\frac{y^{2}}{x^{2}}=\frac{x^{2}}{3}+C$

$y^{2}=\frac{x^{4}}{3}+Cx^{2}$

Curve passes through $(3,3) \Rightarrow C=-2$

$y^{2}=\frac{x^{4}}{3}-2x^{2}$

Which passes through $(\alpha,6\sqrt{10})$

$\frac{\alpha^{4}-6\alpha^{2}}{3}=360$

$\alpha^{4}-6\alpha^{2}-1080=0$

$\alpha=6$

questions.question_text: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $(1-x^{2})dy=(xy+(x^{3}+2)\sqrt{1-x^{2}})dx,-1<x<1$ , and $y(0)=0$ . If $\int_{\frac{-1}{2}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\sqrt{1-x^{2}}y(x)dx=k$ , then k $-$ 1 is equal to _____________.
questions.question_html: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $(1-x^{2})dy=(xy+(x^{3}+2)\sqrt{1-x^{2}})dx,-1<x<1$ , and $y(0)=0$ . If $\int_{\frac{-1}{2}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\sqrt{1-x^{2}}y(x)dx=k$ , then k $-$ 1 is equal to _____________.
questions.explanation_text: $(1-x^{2})dy=(xy+(x^{3}+2)\sqrt{1-x^{2}})dx$ $\therefore$ $\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{x}{1-x^{2}}y=\frac{x^{3}+3}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$ $\therefore$ $I.F.=e^{\int -\frac{x}{1-x^{2}}dx}=\sqrt{1-x^{2}}$ Solution is $y.\sqrt{1-x^{2}}=\int (x^{3}+3)dx$ $y.\sqrt{1-x^{2}}=\frac{x^{4}}{4}+3x+c$ $\because$ $y(0)=0 \Rightarrow c=0$ $\therefore$ $y(x)=\frac{x^{4}+12x}{4\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$ $\therefore$ $\int_{\frac{-1}{2}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\sqrt{1-x^{2}}y(x)dx=\int_{\frac{-1}{2}}^{\frac{1}{2}}(\frac{x^{4}+12x}{4})dx=\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}\frac{x^{4}}{2}dx$ $\therefore$ $k=\frac{1}{320}$ $\therefore$ $=k^{-1}=320$
questions.explanation_html:
$(1-x^{2})dy=(xy+(x^{3}+2)\sqrt{1-x^{2}})dx$

$\therefore$ $\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{x}{1-x^{2}}y=\frac{x^{3}+3}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$

$\therefore$ $I.F.=e^{\int -\frac{x}{1-x^{2}}dx}=\sqrt{1-x^{2}}$

Solution is

$y.\sqrt{1-x^{2}}=\int (x^{3}+3)dx$

$y.\sqrt{1-x^{2}}=\frac{x^{4}}{4}+3x+c$

$\because$ $y(0)=0 \Rightarrow c=0$

$\therefore$ $y(x)=\frac{x^{4}+12x}{4\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$

$\therefore$ $\int_{\frac{-1}{2}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\sqrt{1-x^{2}}y(x)dx=\int_{\frac{-1}{2}}^{\frac{1}{2}}(\frac{x^{4}+12x}{4})dx=\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}\frac{x^{4}}{2}dx$

$\therefore$ $k=\frac{1}{320}$

$\therefore$ $=k^{-1}=320$

questions.question_html: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution curve of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}+(\frac{2x^{2}+11x+13}{x^{3}+6x^{2}+11x+6})y=\frac{(x+3)}{x+1},x>-1$ , which passes through the point $(0,1)$ . Then $y(1)$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $\frac{dy}{dx}+(\frac{2x^{2}+11x+13}{x^{3}+6x^{2}+11x+6})y=\frac{(x+3)}{x+1},x>-1$ , Integrating factor I.F. $=e^{\int \frac{2x^{2}+11x+13}{x^{3}+6x^{2}+11x+6}dx}$ $\begin{aligned} & \text{Let}\frac{2x^{2}+11x+13}{(x+1)(x+2)(x+3)}=\frac{A}{x+1}+\frac{B}{x+2}+\frac{C}{x+3} \\ \\ & A=2,B=1,C=-1 \\ \\ & \text{I.F.}=e^{(2ln|x+1|+ln|x+2|-ln|x+3|)} \\ \\ & =\frac{(x+1)^{2}(x+2)}{x+3} \end{aligned}$ Solution of differential equation $\begin{aligned} & y \cdot \frac{(x+1)^{2}(x+2)}{x+3}=\int (x+1)(x+2)dx \\ \\ & y\frac{(x+1)^{2}(x+2)}{x+3}=\frac{x^{3}}{3}+\frac{3x^{2}}{2}+2x+c \end{aligned}$ Curve passes through $(0,1)$ $\begin{aligned} 1 \times \frac{1 \times 2}{3}=0+c \Rightarrow c=\frac{2}{3} \\ \\ \text{So,}y(1)=\frac{\frac{1}{3}+\frac{3}{2}+2+\frac{2}{3}}{\frac{(2^{2} \times 3)}{4}}=\frac{3}{2} \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\frac{dy}{dx}+(\frac{2x^{2}+11x+13}{x^{3}+6x^{2}+11x+6})y=\frac{(x+3)}{x+1},x>-1$ ,

Integrating factor I.F. $=e^{\int \frac{2x^{2}+11x+13}{x^{3}+6x^{2}+11x+6}dx}$

$\begin{aligned} & \text{Let}\frac{2x^{2}+11x+13}{(x+1)(x+2)(x+3)}=\frac{A}{x+1}+\frac{B}{x+2}+\frac{C}{x+3} \\ \\ & A=2,B=1,C=-1 \\ \\ & \text{I.F.}=e^{(2ln|x+1|+ln|x+2|-ln|x+3|)} \\ \\ & =\frac{(x+1)^{2}(x+2)}{x+3} \end{aligned}$

Solution of differential equation

$\begin{aligned} & y \cdot \frac{(x+1)^{2}(x+2)}{x+3}=\int (x+1)(x+2)dx \\ \\ & y\frac{(x+1)^{2}(x+2)}{x+3}=\frac{x^{3}}{3}+\frac{3x^{2}}{2}+2x+c \end{aligned}$

Curve passes through $(0,1)$

$\begin{aligned} 1 \times \frac{1 \times 2}{3}=0+c \Rightarrow c=\frac{2}{3} \\ \\ \text{So,}y(1)=\frac{\frac{1}{3}+\frac{3}{2}+2+\frac{2}{3}}{\frac{(2^{2} \times 3)}{4}}=\frac{3}{2} \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html: Let the solution curve of the differential equation $xdy=(\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}+y)dx,x>0$ , intersect the line $x=1$ at $y=0$ and the line $x=2$ at $y=\alpha$ . Then the value of $\alpha$ is :

at $x=1,y=0$

questions.question_html: If $\frac{dy}{dx}+2ytanx=sinx,0<x<\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $y(\frac{\pi}{3})=0$ , then the maximum value of $y(x)$ is :
questions.explanation_text: $\frac{dy}{dx}+2ytanx=sinx$ which is a first order linear differential equation. Integrating factor (I. F.) $=e^{\int 2tanxdx}$ $=e^{2ln|secx|}=sec^{2}x$ Solution of differential equation can be written as $y.sec^{2}x=\int sinx.sec^{2}xdx=\int secx.tanxdx$ $ysec^{2}x=secx+C$ $y(\frac{\pi}{3})=0,0=sec\frac{\pi}{3}+C \Rightarrow C=-2$ $y=\frac{secx-2}{sec^{2}x}=cosx-2cos^{2}x$ $=\frac{1}{8}-2(cosx-\frac{1}{4})^{2}$ $y_{max}=\frac{1}{8}$

questions.question_text: Let $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{ax-by+a}{bx+cy+a},a,b,c \in R$ , represents a circle with center ( $\alpha$ , $\beta$ ). Then, $\alpha$ + 2 $\beta$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{ax-by+a}{bx+cy+a},a,b,c \in R$ , represents a circle with center ( $\alpha$ , $\beta$ ). Then, $\alpha$ + 2 $\beta$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Given, $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{ax-by+a}{bx+cy+a}$ $\Rightarrow bxdy+cydy+ady=axdx-bydx+adx$ $\Rightarrow bxdy+bydx+(cy+a)dy=(ax+a)dx$ $\Rightarrow b(xdy+ydx)+(cy+a)dy=(ax+a)dx$ $\Rightarrow bd(xy)+(cy+a)dy=(ax+a)dx$ Integrating both sides, we get $\Rightarrow b\int d(xy)+\int (cy+a)dy=\int (ax+a)dx$ $\Rightarrow b.xy+c.\frac{y^{2}}{2}+ay=\frac{ax^{2}}{2}+ax+k$ $\Rightarrow \frac{ax^{2}}{2}-\frac{cy^{2}}{2}-bxy+ax-ay+k=0$ For equation of circle, Coefficient of x 2 = Coefficient of y 2 $\therefore$ $\frac{a}{2}=-\frac{c}{2}$ $\Rightarrow a=-c$ And coefficient of $xy=0$ $\therefore$ $-b=0$ $\Rightarrow b=0$ $\therefore$ Circle equation becomes, $\frac{ax^{2}}{2}+\frac{ay^{2}}{2}+ax-ay+k=0$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}+2x-2y+\frac{2k}{a}=0$ $\therefore$ Center $=(-g,-f)=(-1,1)=(\alpha,\beta)$ $\therefore$ $\alpha=-1$ and $\beta=1$ $\therefore$ $\alpha+2\beta=-1+2 \times (1)=1$
questions.explanation_html:
Given,

$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{ax-by+a}{bx+cy+a}$

$\Rightarrow bxdy+cydy+ady=axdx-bydx+adx$

$\Rightarrow bxdy+bydx+(cy+a)dy=(ax+a)dx$

$\Rightarrow b(xdy+ydx)+(cy+a)dy=(ax+a)dx$

$\Rightarrow bd(xy)+(cy+a)dy=(ax+a)dx$

Integrating both sides, we get

$\Rightarrow b\int d(xy)+\int (cy+a)dy=\int (ax+a)dx$

$\Rightarrow b.xy+c.\frac{y^{2}}{2}+ay=\frac{ax^{2}}{2}+ax+k$

$\Rightarrow \frac{ax^{2}}{2}-\frac{cy^{2}}{2}-bxy+ax-ay+k=0$

For equation of circle,

Coefficient of x2 = Coefficient of y2

$\therefore$ $\frac{a}{2}=-\frac{c}{2}$

$\Rightarrow a=-c$

And coefficient of $xy=0$

$\therefore$ $-b=0$

$\Rightarrow b=0$

$\therefore$ Circle equation becomes,

$\frac{ax^{2}}{2}+\frac{ay^{2}}{2}+ax-ay+k=0$

$\Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}+2x-2y+\frac{2k}{a}=0$

$\therefore$ Center $=(-g,-f)=(-1,1)=(\alpha,\beta)$

$\therefore$ $\alpha=-1$ and $\beta=1$

$\therefore$ $\alpha+2\beta=-1+2 \times (1)=1$

questions.question_html: Let $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{ax-by+a}{bx+cy+a}$ , where a, b, c are constants, represent a circle passing through the point (2, 5). Then the shortest distance of the point (11, 6) from this circle is :
questions.explanation_text: $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{ax-by+a}{bx+cy+a}$ $=bxdy+cydy+ady=axdx-bydx+adx$ $=cydy+ady-axdx-adx+b(xdy+ydx)=0$ $=c\int ydy+a\int xdx-a\int dx+b\int d(xy)=0$ $=\frac{cy^{2}}{2}+ay-\frac{ax^{2}}{2}-ax+bxy=k$ $=ax^{2}-cy^{2}+2ax-2ay-2bxy=k$ Above equation is circle $\Rightarrow$ a = $-$ c and b = 0 $ax^{2}+ay^{2}+2ax-2ay=k$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}+2x-2y=\lambda[\lambda=\frac{k}{a}]$ Passes through (2, 5) $4+25+4-10=\lambda \Rightarrow \lambda=23$ Circle $\equiv x^{2}+y^{2}+2x-2y-23=0$ Centre ( $-$ 1, 1) $r=\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+1^{2}+23}=5$ Shortest distance of $(11,6)=\sqrt{12^{2}+5^{2}}-5$ $=13-5$ $=8$
questions.explanation_html:
$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{ax-by+a}{bx+cy+a}$

$=bxdy+cydy+ady=axdx-bydx+adx$

$=cydy+ady-axdx-adx+b(xdy+ydx)=0$

$=c\int ydy+a\int xdx-a\int dx+b\int d(xy)=0$

$=\frac{cy^{2}}{2}+ay-\frac{ax^{2}}{2}-ax+bxy=k$

$=ax^{2}-cy^{2}+2ax-2ay-2bxy=k$

Above equation is circle

$\Rightarrow$ a = $-$ c and b = 0

$ax^{2}+ay^{2}+2ax-2ay=k$

$\Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}+2x-2y=\lambda[\lambda=\frac{k}{a}]$

Passes through (2, 5)

$4+25+4-10=\lambda \Rightarrow \lambda=23$

Circle $\equiv x^{2}+y^{2}+2x-2y-23=0$

Centre ( $-$ 1, 1) $r=\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+1^{2}+23}=5$

Shortest distance of $(11,6)=\sqrt{12^{2}+5^{2}}-5$

$=13-5$

$=8$

questions.explanation_text: $\frac{dx}{dy}-\frac{2x}{y}=y^{2}(y+1)e^{y}$ $\text{If}=e^{\int -\frac{2}{y}dy}=e^{-2lny}=\frac{1}{y^{2}}$ Solution is given by $\begin{aligned} & x \cdot \frac{1}{y^{2}}=\int y^{2}(y+1)e^{y} \cdot \frac{1}{y^{2}}dy \\ \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{x}{y^{2}}=\int (y+1)e^{y}dy \\ \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{x}{y^{2}}=ye^{y}+c \end{aligned}$ $\Rightarrow x=y^{2}(ye^{y}+c)$ at, $y=1,x=0$ $\Rightarrow 0=1(1 \cdot e^{1}+c) \Rightarrow c=-e$ at $y=e$ , $x=e^{2}(e.e^{e}-e)$
