questions.question_text: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{4y^{3}+2yx^{2}}{3xy^{2}+x^{3}},y(1)=1$ . If for some $n \in ℕ,y(2) \in [n-1,n)$ , then $n$ is equal to _____________.
questions.question_html:
Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation

$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{4y^{3}+2yx^{2}}{3xy^{2}+x^{3}},y(1)=1$ .

If for some $n \in ℕ,y(2) \in [n-1,n)$ , then $n$ is equal to _____________.
questions.explanation_text: $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y}{x}\frac{(4y^{2}+2x^{2})}{(3y^{2}+x^{2})}$ Put $y=vx$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=v+x\frac{dv}{dx}$ $\Rightarrow v+x\frac{dv}{dx}=\frac{v(4v^{2}+2)}{(3v^{2}+1)}$ $\Rightarrow x\frac{dv}{dx}=v(\frac{(4v^{2}+2-3v^{2}-1)}{3v^{2}+1})$ $\Rightarrow \int (3v^{2}+1)\frac{dv}{v^{3}+v}=\int \frac{dx}{x}$ $\Rightarrow ln|v^{3}+v|=lnx+c$ $\Rightarrow ln|(\frac{y}{x})^{3}+(\frac{y}{x})|=lnx+C$ $↓y(1)=1$ $\Rightarrow C=ln2$ $\therefore$ for $y(2)$ $ln(\frac{y^{3}}{8}+\frac{y}{2})=2ln2 \Rightarrow \frac{y^{3}}{8}+\frac{y}{2}=4$ $\Rightarrow [y(2)]=2$ $\Rightarrow n=3$
questions.explanation_html:
$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y}{x}\frac{(4y^{2}+2x^{2})}{(3y^{2}+x^{2})}$

Put $y=vx$

$\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=v+x\frac{dv}{dx}$

$\Rightarrow v+x\frac{dv}{dx}=\frac{v(4v^{2}+2)}{(3v^{2}+1)}$

$\Rightarrow x\frac{dv}{dx}=v(\frac{(4v^{2}+2-3v^{2}-1)}{3v^{2}+1})$

$\Rightarrow \int (3v^{2}+1)\frac{dv}{v^{3}+v}=\int \frac{dx}{x}$

$\Rightarrow ln|v^{3}+v|=lnx+c$

$\Rightarrow ln|(\frac{y}{x})^{3}+(\frac{y}{x})|=lnx+C$

$↓y(1)=1$

$\Rightarrow C=ln2$

$\therefore$ for $y(2)$

$ln(\frac{y^{3}}{8}+\frac{y}{2})=2ln2 \Rightarrow \frac{y^{3}}{8}+\frac{y}{2}=4$

$\Rightarrow [y(2)]=2$

$\Rightarrow n=3$

If $e^{\int \frac{1}{x^{2}}dx}=e^{-\frac{1}{x}}$

$y(\frac{1}{2})=3-\frac{1}{e} \times e^{2}$

$y(\frac{1}{2})=3-e$

questions.explanation_text: $xdy=(y+x^{3}cosx)dx$ $\Rightarrow$ $xdy=ydx+x^{3}cosxdx$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{xdy-ydx}{x^{2}}=\frac{x^{3}coxdx}{x^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{d}{dx}(\frac{y}{x})=\int xcosxdx$ $\Rightarrow \frac{y}{x}=xsinx-\int 1.sinxdx$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{y}{x}=xsinx+cosx+C$ $\Rightarrow 0=-1+C \Rightarrow C=1,x=\pi,y=0$ so, $\frac{y}{x}=xsinx+cosx+1$ $y=x^{2}sinx+xcosx+x$ $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ $y(\frac{\pi}{2})=\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}+\frac{\pi}{2}$

questions.explanation_text: We have, $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x(\frac{y}{x}.tan\frac{y}{x}-1)}{xtan\frac{y}{x}}$ $\therefore$ $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y}{x}-cot(\frac{y}{x})$ Put $\frac{y}{x}=v$ $\Rightarrow y=vn$ $\therefore$ $\frac{dy}{dx}=v+\frac{ndv}{dx}$ Now, we get $v+n\frac{dv}{dx}=v-cot(v)$ $\Rightarrow \int (tan)dv=-\int \frac{dx}{x}$ $\therefore$ $ln|sec(\frac{y}{x})|=-ln|x|+c$ As, $(\frac{1}{2})=(\frac{y}{x}) \Rightarrow C=0$ $\therefore$ $sec(\frac{y}{x})=\frac{1}{x}$ $\Rightarrow cos(\frac{y}{x})=x$ $\therefore$ $y=xcos^{-1}(x)$ So, required bounded area $=\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}\underset{(II)}{x}(\underset{(I)}{cos^{-1}x})dx=(\frac{\pi-1}{8})$ (I. B. P.) $\therefore$ Option (1) is correct.
questions.explanation_html:
We have,

$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x(\frac{y}{x}.tan\frac{y}{x}-1)}{xtan\frac{y}{x}}$

Put $\frac{y}{x}=v$

$\Rightarrow y=vn$

$\therefore$ $\frac{dy}{dx}=v+\frac{ndv}{dx}$

Now, we get

$v+n\frac{dv}{dx}=v-cot(v)$

As, $(\frac{1}{2})=(\frac{y}{x}) \Rightarrow C=0$

$\Rightarrow cos(\frac{y}{x})=x$

$\therefore$ $y=xcos^{-1}(x)$

So, required bounded area

$=\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}\underset{(II)}{x}(\underset{(I)}{cos^{-1}x})dx=(\frac{\pi-1}{8})$ (I. B. P.)

$y^{\frac{1}{4}}+\frac{1}{y^{\frac{1}{4}}}=2x$

$\Rightarrow (y^{\frac{1}{4}})^{2}-2xy^{(\frac{1}{4})}+1=0$

$\Rightarrow y^{\frac{1}{4}}=x+\sqrt{x^{2}-1}$ or $x-\sqrt{x^{2}-1}$

So, $\frac{1}{4}\frac{1}{y^{\frac{3}{4}}}\frac{dy}{dx}=1+\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^{2}-1}}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{4}\frac{1}{y^{\frac{3}{4}}}\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y^{\frac{1}{4}}}{\sqrt{x^{2}-1}}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{4y}{\sqrt{x^{2}-1}}$ .... (1)

Hence, $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=4\frac{(\sqrt{x^{2}-1})y^{'}-\frac{yx}{\sqrt{x^{2}-1}}}{x^{2}-1}$

$\Rightarrow (x^{2}-1)y^{''}=4\frac{(x^{2}-1)y^{'}-xy}{\sqrt{x^{2}-1}}$

$\Rightarrow (x^{2}-1)y^{''}=4(\sqrt{x^{2}-1}y^{'}-\frac{xy}{\sqrt{x^{2}-1}})$

$\Rightarrow (x^{2}-1)y^{''}=4(4y-\frac{xy^{'}}{4})$ (from I)

$\Rightarrow (x^{2}-1)y^{''}+xy^{'}-16y=0$

So, | $\alpha$ $-$ $\beta$ | = 17

questions.explanation_text: $\frac{dy}{dx}+2sin^{2}x=1+ycos2x$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}+(-cos2x)y=cos2x$ $I.F.=e^{\int -cos2xdx}=e^{-\frac{sin2x}{2}}$ Solution of D.E. $y(e^{-\frac{sin2x}{2}})=\int (cos2x)(e^{-\frac{sin2x}{2}})dx+c$ $\Rightarrow y(e^{-\frac{sin2x}{2}})=-e^{-\frac{sin2x}{2}}+c$ Given $y(\frac{\pi}{4})=0$ $\Rightarrow 0=-e^{\frac{-1}{2}}+c \Rightarrow c=e^{\frac{-1}{2}}$ $\Rightarrow y(e^{-\frac{sin2x}{2}})=-e^{-\frac{sin2x}{2}}+e^{\frac{-1}{2}}$ at x = 0 $y=-1+e^{\frac{-1}{2}}$ $\Rightarrow y(0)=-1+e^{\frac{-1}{2}} \Rightarrow (y(0)+1)^{2}=e^{-1}$

questions.question_html:
Let y = y(x) be the solution of the differential equation

$\frac{dy}{dx}=(y+1)((y+1)e^{x^{2}/2}-x)$ , 0 < x < 2.1, with y(2) = 0. Then the value of $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at x = 1 is equal to :
questions.explanation_html:
$\frac{dy}{dx}=(y+1)((y+1)e^{\frac{x^{2}}{2}}-x)$

$\Rightarrow \frac{-1}{(y+1)^{2}}\frac{dy}{dx}-x(\frac{1}{y+1})=-e^{\frac{x^{2}}{2}}$

Put, $\frac{1}{y+1}=z$

$-\frac{1}{(y+1)^{2}}.\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dz}{dx}$

$\therefore$ $\frac{dz}{dx}+z(-x)=-e^{\frac{x^{2}}{2}}$

$I.F=e^{\int -xdx}=e^{\frac{-x^{2}}{2}}$

$z.(e^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2}})=-\int e^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2}}.e^{\frac{x^{2}}{2}}dx=-\int 1.dx=-x+C$

$\Rightarrow \frac{e^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2}}}{y+1}=-x+C$ .... (1)

Given y = 0 at x = 2 Put in (1)

$\frac{e^{-2}}{0+1}=-2+C$

$C=e^{-2}+2$ .... (2)

From (1) and (2)

$y+1=\frac{e^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2}}}{e^{-2}+2-x}$

Again, at x = 1

$\Rightarrow y+1=\frac{e^{3/2}}{e^{2}+1}$

$\Rightarrow y+1=\frac{e^{3/2}}{e^{2}+1}$

$\therefore$ $\frac{dy}{dx}|_{x=1}=\frac{e^{3/2}}{e^{2}+1}(\frac{e^{3/2}}{e^{2}+1} \times e^{1/2}-1)$

$=-\frac{e^{3/2}}{(e^{2}+1)^{2}}$

questions.question_html: The rate of growth of bacteria in a culture is proportional to the number of bacteria present and the bacteria count is 1000 at initial time t = 0. The number of bacteria is increased by 20% in 2 hours. If the population of bacteria is 2000 after $\frac{k}{log_{e}(\frac{6}{5})}$ hours, then $(\frac{k}{log_{e}2})^{2}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $\frac{dx}{dt}∝x$ $\frac{dx}{dt}=\lambda x$ $\int_{1000}^{x}\frac{dx}{x}=\int_{0}^{t}\lambda dt$ $lnx-ln1000=\lambda t$ $ln(\frac{x}{1000})=\lambda t$ Put t = 2, x = 1200 $ln(\frac{12}{10})=2\lambda \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{1}{2}ln\frac{6}{5}$ Now, $ln(\frac{x}{1000})=\frac{t}{2}ln(\frac{6}{5})$ $x=1000e^{\frac{t}{2}ln(\frac{6}{5})}$ $x=2000$ at $t=\frac{k}{ln(\frac{6}{5})}$ $\Rightarrow 2000=1000e^{\frac{k}{2ln(6/5)} \times ln(6/5)}$ $\Rightarrow 2=e^{k/2}$ $\Rightarrow ln2=\frac{k}{2}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{k}{ln2}=2$ $\Rightarrow (\frac{k}{ln2})^{2}=4$
questions.explanation_html:
$\frac{dx}{dt}∝x$

$\frac{dx}{dt}=\lambda x$

$\int_{1000}^{x}\frac{dx}{x}=\int_{0}^{t}\lambda dt$

$lnx-ln1000=\lambda t$

$ln(\frac{x}{1000})=\lambda t$

Put t = 2, x = 1200

$ln(\frac{12}{10})=2\lambda \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{1}{2}ln\frac{6}{5}$

Now, $ln(\frac{x}{1000})=\frac{t}{2}ln(\frac{6}{5})$

$x=1000e^{\frac{t}{2}ln(\frac{6}{5})}$

$x=2000$ at $t=\frac{k}{ln(\frac{6}{5})}$

$\Rightarrow 2000=1000e^{\frac{k}{2ln(6/5)} \times ln(6/5)}$

$\Rightarrow 2=e^{k/2}$

$\Rightarrow ln2=\frac{k}{2}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{k}{ln2}=2$

$\Rightarrow (\frac{k}{ln2})^{2}=4$

questions.question_html: Let y = y(x) be the solution of the differential equation $((x+2)e^{(\frac{y+1}{x+2})}+(y+1))dx=(x+2)dy$ , y(1) = 1. If the domain of y = y(x) is an open interval ( $\alpha$ , $\beta$ ), then | $\alpha$ + $\beta$ | is equal to ______________.
questions.explanation_text: Let y + 1 = Y and x + 2 = X dy = dY dx = dX $(Xe^{\frac{X}{X}}+Y)dX=XdY$ $\Rightarrow \frac{XdY-YdX}{X^{2}}=\frac{e^{\frac{Y}{X}}}{X}dX$ $\Rightarrow e^{-\frac{Y}{X}}d(\frac{Y}{X})=\frac{dX}{X}$ $\Rightarrow -e^{-\frac{Y}{X}}=ln|X|+c$ $\Rightarrow -e^{-(\frac{y+1}{x+2})}=ln|x+2|+c$ $\because$ (1, 1) satisfy this equation So, $c=-e^{-\frac{2}{3}}-ln3$ Now, $y=-1-(x+2)ln(ln(|\frac{3}{x+2}|)+e^{-\frac{2}{3}})$ Domain : $ln|\frac{3}{x+2}|>e^{-e^{-\frac{2}{3}}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{3}{|x+2|}>e^{-e^{-\frac{2}{3}}}$ $\Rightarrow |x+2|<3e^{e^{-\frac{2}{3}}}$ $\Rightarrow -3e^{e^{-\frac{2}{3}}}-2<x<3e^{e^{-\frac{2}{3}}}-2$ So, $\alpha+\beta=-4$ $\Rightarrow |\alpha+\beta|=4$
questions.explanation_html:
Let y + 1 = Y and x + 2 = X

dy = dY

dx = dX

$(Xe^{\frac{X}{X}}+Y)dX=XdY$

$\Rightarrow \frac{XdY-YdX}{X^{2}}=\frac{e^{\frac{Y}{X}}}{X}dX$

$\Rightarrow e^{-\frac{Y}{X}}d(\frac{Y}{X})=\frac{dX}{X}$

$\Rightarrow -e^{-\frac{Y}{X}}=ln|X|+c$

$\Rightarrow -e^{-(\frac{y+1}{x+2})}=ln|x+2|+c$

$\because$ (1, 1) satisfy this equation

So, $c=-e^{-\frac{2}{3}}-ln3$

Now, $y=-1-(x+2)ln(ln(|\frac{3}{x+2}|)+e^{-\frac{2}{3}})$

Domain :

$ln|\frac{3}{x+2}|>e^{-e^{-\frac{2}{3}}}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{3}{|x+2|}>e^{-e^{-\frac{2}{3}}}$

$\Rightarrow |x+2|<3e^{e^{-\frac{2}{3}}}$

$\Rightarrow -3e^{e^{-\frac{2}{3}}}-2<x<3e^{e^{-\frac{2}{3}}}-2$

So, $\alpha+\beta=-4$

$\Rightarrow |\alpha+\beta|=4$

questions.question_html: The difference between degree and order of a differential equation that represents the family of curves given by $y^{2}=a(x+\frac{\sqrt{a}}{2})$ , a > 0 is _________.
questions.explanation_text: $y^{2}=a(x+\frac{\sqrt{a}}{2})$ Differentiating both sides, we get $2yy^{'}=a$ $y^{2}=2yy^{'}(x+\frac{\sqrt{2yy^{'}}}{2})$ $y=2y^{'}(x+\frac{\sqrt{yy^{'}}}{\sqrt{2}})$ $y-2xy^{'}=\sqrt{2}y^{'}\sqrt{yy^{'}}$ $(y-2x\frac{dy}{dx})^{2}=2y(\frac{dy}{dx})^{3}$ D = 3 & O = 1 $\therefore$ D $-$ O = 3 $-$ 1 = 2
questions.explanation_html:
$y^{2}=a(x+\frac{\sqrt{a}}{2})$

Differentiating both sides, we get

$2yy^{'}=a$

$y^{2}=2yy^{'}(x+\frac{\sqrt{2yy^{'}}}{2})$

$y=2y^{'}(x+\frac{\sqrt{yy^{'}}}{\sqrt{2}})$

$y-2xy^{'}=\sqrt{2}y^{'}\sqrt{yy^{'}}$

$(y-2x\frac{dy}{dx})^{2}=2y(\frac{dy}{dx})^{3}$

D = 3 & O = 1

questions.explanation_text: $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2^{x+y}-2^{x}}{2^{y}}$ $2^{y}\frac{dy}{dx}=2^{x}(2^{y}-1)$ $\int \frac{2^{y}}{2^{y}-1}dy=\int 2^{x}dx$ $\frac{ln(2^{y}-1)}{ln2}=\frac{2^{x}}{ln2}+C$ $\Rightarrow log_{2}(2^{y}-1)=2^{x}log_{2}e+C$ $\because$ $y(0)=1 \Rightarrow 0=log_{2}e+C$ $C=-log_{2}e$ $\Rightarrow log_{2}(2^{y}-1)=(2^{x}-1)log_{2}e$ put x = 1, $log_{2}(2^{y}-1)=log_{2}e$ 2 y = e + 1 y = log 2 (e + 1) Ans.
questions.explanation_html:
$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2^{x+y}-2^{x}}{2^{y}}$

questions.explanation_text: $cos(\frac{1}{2}cos^{-1}(e^{-x}))dx=\sqrt{e^{2x}-1}dy$ Put cos $-$ 1 (e $-$ x ) $\theta$ , $\theta$ $\in$ [0, $\pi$ ] $cos\theta=e^{-x} \Rightarrow 2cos^{2}\frac{\theta}{2}-1=e^{-x}$ $cos\frac{\theta}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{e^{-x}+1}{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{e^{x}+1}{2c^{x}}}$ $\sqrt{\frac{e^{x}+1}{2c^{x}}}dx=\sqrt{e^{2x}-1}dy$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{e^{x}}\sqrt{e^{x}-1}}=\int dy$ Put $e^{x}=t,\frac{dt}{dx}=e^{x}$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\int \frac{dx}{e^{x}\sqrt{e^{x}}\sqrt{e^{x}-1}}=\int dy$ $\int \frac{dt}{t\sqrt{t^{2}-t}}=\sqrt{2}y$ Put $t=\frac{1}{z},\frac{dt}{dz}=-\frac{1}{z^{2}}$ $\int \frac{-\frac{dz}{z^{2}}}{\frac{1}{z}\sqrt{\frac{1}{z^{2}}-\frac{1}{z}}}=\sqrt{2y}$ $-\int \frac{dz}{\sqrt{1-z}}=\sqrt{2}y$ $\frac{-2(1-z)^{1/2}}{-1}=\sqrt{2}y+c$ $2(1-\frac{1}{t})^{1/2}=\sqrt{2}y+c$ $2(1-e^{-x})^{1/2}=\sqrt{2}y+c\bar{\longrightarrow} \Rightarrow c=\sqrt{2}$ $2(1-e^{-x})^{1/2}=\sqrt{2}(y+1)$ , passes through ( $\alpha$ , 0) $2(1-e^{-\alpha})^{1/2}=\sqrt{2}$ $\sqrt{1-e^{-\alpha}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Rightarrow 1-e^{-\alpha}=\frac{1}{2}$ $e^{-\alpha}=\frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow e^{\alpha}=2$
questions.explanation_html:
$cos(\frac{1}{2}cos^{-1}(e^{-x}))dx=\sqrt{e^{2x}-1}dy$

Put cos $-$ 1(e $-$ x) $\theta$ , $\theta$ $\in$ [0, $\pi$ ]

$cos\theta=e^{-x} \Rightarrow 2cos^{2}\frac{\theta}{2}-1=e^{-x}$

$cos\frac{\theta}{2}=\sqrt{\frac{e^{-x}+1}{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{e^{x}+1}{2c^{x}}}$

$\sqrt{\frac{e^{x}+1}{2c^{x}}}dx=\sqrt{e^{2x}-1}dy$

$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{e^{x}}\sqrt{e^{x}-1}}=\int dy$

Put $e^{x}=t,\frac{dt}{dx}=e^{x}$

$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\int \frac{dx}{e^{x}\sqrt{e^{x}}\sqrt{e^{x}-1}}=\int dy$

$\int \frac{dt}{t\sqrt{t^{2}-t}}=\sqrt{2}y$

Put $t=\frac{1}{z},\frac{dt}{dz}=-\frac{1}{z^{2}}$

$\int \frac{-\frac{dz}{z^{2}}}{\frac{1}{z}\sqrt{\frac{1}{z^{2}}-\frac{1}{z}}}=\sqrt{2y}$

$-\int \frac{dz}{\sqrt{1-z}}=\sqrt{2}y$

$\frac{-2(1-z)^{1/2}}{-1}=\sqrt{2}y+c$

$2(1-\frac{1}{t})^{1/2}=\sqrt{2}y+c$

$2(1-e^{-x})^{1/2}=\sqrt{2}y+c\bar{\longrightarrow} \Rightarrow c=\sqrt{2}$

$2(1-e^{-x})^{1/2}=\sqrt{2}(y+1)$ , passes through ( $\alpha$ , 0)

$2(1-e^{-\alpha})^{1/2}=\sqrt{2}$

$\sqrt{1-e^{-\alpha}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Rightarrow 1-e^{-\alpha}=\frac{1}{2}$

$e^{-\alpha}=\frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow e^{\alpha}=2$

If for x $\ge$ 0, y = y(x) is the solution of the
differential equation (x + 1)dy = ((x + 1) 2 + y – 3)dx, y(2) = 0,
then y(3) is equal to _______.
questions.question_html:
If for x $\ge$ 0, y = y(x) is the solution of the differential equation
(x + 1)dy = ((x + 1)2 + y – 3)dx, y(2) = 0, then y(3) is equal to _______.
questions.explanation_text: (x + 1)dy = ((x + 1) 2 + y – 3)dx $\Rightarrow$ (1 + x) $\frac{dy}{dx}$ - y = (1 + x) 2 - 3 $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{y}{1+x}=(1+x)-\frac{3}{1+x}$ I.F = $e^{-\int \frac{dx}{1+x}}$ = $\frac{1}{1+x}$ Solution of the differential equation, $y(\frac{1}{1+x})$ = $\int ((1+x)-\frac{3}{1+x})(\frac{1}{1+x})dx$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{y}{1+x}$ = $\int \frac{x^{2}+2x+1-3}{(x+1)^{2}}dx$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{y}{1+x}$ = x + $\frac{3}{1+x}$ + C As y(2) = 0 $\Rightarrow$ x = 2, y = 0 $\therefore$ 0 = 2 + $\frac{3}{1+2}$ + C $\Rightarrow$ C = -3 So solution is $\frac{y}{1+x}$ = x + $\frac{3}{1+x}$ - 3 y(3) means x = 3 and find value of y. $\frac{y}{1+3}=3+\frac{3}{1+3}-3$ $\Rightarrow$ y = 3
questions.explanation_html:
(x + 1)dy = ((x + 1)2 + y – 3)dx

$\Rightarrow$ (1 + x) $\frac{dy}{dx}$ - y = (1 + x)2 - 3

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{y}{1+x}=(1+x)-\frac{3}{1+x}$

I.F = $e^{-\int \frac{dx}{1+x}}$ = $\frac{1}{1+x}$

Solution of the differential equation,

$y(\frac{1}{1+x})$ = $\int ((1+x)-\frac{3}{1+x})(\frac{1}{1+x})dx$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{y}{1+x}$ = $\int \frac{x^{2}+2x+1-3}{(x+1)^{2}}dx$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{y}{1+x}$ = x + $\frac{3}{1+x}$ + C

As y(2) = 0 $\Rightarrow$ x = 2, y = 0

$\therefore$ 0 = 2 + $\frac{3}{1+2}$ + C

$\Rightarrow$ C = -3

So solution is $\frac{y}{1+x}$ = x + $\frac{3}{1+x}$ - 3

y(3) means x = 3 and find value of y.

$\frac{y}{1+3}=3+\frac{3}{1+3}-3$

$\Rightarrow$ y = 3

questions.question_text:
If a curve y = f(x), passing through the point
(1, 2), is the solution of the differential equation, 2x 2 dy= (2xy + y 2 )dx, then $f(\frac{1}{2})$ is equal to :
questions.question_html:
If a curve y = f(x), passing through the point (1, 2), is the solution of the differential equation,
2x2dy= (2xy + y2)dx, then $f(\frac{1}{2})$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $2x^{2}dy=(2xy+y^{2})dx$ $\Rightarrow 2x^{2}\frac{dy}{dx}=2xy+y^{2}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{2x^{2}}{2x^{2}y^{2}}\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2xy}{2x^{2}y^{2}}+\frac{y^{2}}{2x^{2}y^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{y^{2}}\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{1}{x}\frac{1}{y}=\frac{1}{2x^{2}}$ Let $-\frac{1}{y}=t$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{y^{2}}\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dt}{dx}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dt}{dx}+t\frac{1}{x}=\frac{1}{2x^{2}}$ This is linear differentiatial equation. $\therefore I.F=e^{\int \frac{1}{x}dx}=e^{lnx}$ $\therefore t.e^{lnx}=\int \frac{1}{2x^{2}}.e^{lnx}dx$ $\Rightarrow -\frac{1}{y}.x=\int \frac{1}{2x^{2}}.xdx$ $\Rightarrow -\frac{x}{y}=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{dx}{x}$ $\Rightarrow -\frac{x}{y}=\frac{1}{2}lnx+c$ This curve passes through the point (1, 2) $\therefore -\frac{1}{2}=0+c$ $\Rightarrow c=-\frac{1}{2}$ $\therefore -\frac{x}{y}=\frac{1}{2}lnx-\frac{1}{2}$ $\Rightarrow -\frac{2x}{y}=lnx-1$ $\Rightarrow y=\frac{2x}{1-lnx}$ $\Rightarrow f(x)=\frac{2x}{1-lnx}$ So, $f(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{2 \times \frac{1}{2}}{1-ln(\frac{1}{2})}=\frac{1}{1+log_{e}2}$
questions.explanation_html:
$2x^{2}dy=(2xy+y^{2})dx$

$\Rightarrow 2x^{2}\frac{dy}{dx}=2xy+y^{2}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{2x^{2}}{2x^{2}y^{2}}\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2xy}{2x^{2}y^{2}}+\frac{y^{2}}{2x^{2}y^{2}}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{y^{2}}\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{1}{x}\frac{1}{y}=\frac{1}{2x^{2}}$

Let $-\frac{1}{y}=t$

$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{y^{2}}\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dt}{dx}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{dt}{dx}+t\frac{1}{x}=\frac{1}{2x^{2}}$

This is linear differentiatial equation.

$\therefore I.F=e^{\int \frac{1}{x}dx}=e^{lnx}$

$\therefore t.e^{lnx}=\int \frac{1}{2x^{2}}.e^{lnx}dx$

$\Rightarrow -\frac{1}{y}.x=\int \frac{1}{2x^{2}}.xdx$

$\Rightarrow -\frac{x}{y}=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{dx}{x}$

$\Rightarrow -\frac{x}{y}=\frac{1}{2}lnx+c$

This curve passes through the point (1, 2)

$\therefore -\frac{1}{2}=0+c$

$\Rightarrow c=-\frac{1}{2}$

$\therefore -\frac{x}{y}=\frac{1}{2}lnx-\frac{1}{2}$

$\Rightarrow -\frac{2x}{y}=lnx-1$

$\Rightarrow y=\frac{2x}{1-lnx}$

$\Rightarrow f(x)=\frac{2x}{1-lnx}$

So, $f(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{2 \times \frac{1}{2}}{1-ln(\frac{1}{2})}=\frac{1}{1+log_{e}2}$

Let y = y(x) be a solution of the differential
equation, $\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\frac{dy}{dx}+\sqrt{1-y^{2}}=0$ , |x| < 1. If $y(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ , then $y(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})$ is equal to :
questions.question_html:
Let y = y(x) be a solution of the differential equation,

$\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\frac{dy}{dx}+\sqrt{1-y^{2}}=0$ , |x| < 1.

If $y(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ , then $y(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})$ is equal to :

options.label: B
options.html: None of those

questions.explanation_text: Given $\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\frac{dy}{dx}+\sqrt{1-y^{2}}=0$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{\sqrt{1-y^{2}}}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{dy}{\sqrt{1-y^{2}}}+\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}=0$ $\Rightarrow$ sin -1 y + sin -1 x = c Given that $y(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ So when x = $\frac{1}{2}$ then y = $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ $\therefore$ sin -1 $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ + sin -1 $\frac{1}{2}$ = c $\Rightarrow$ c = $\frac{\pi}{3}$ + $\frac{\pi}{6}$ = $\frac{\pi}{2}$ So sin -1 y + sin -1 x = $\frac{\pi}{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ sin -1 y = $\frac{\pi}{2}$ - sin -1 x $\Rightarrow$ sin -1 y = cos -1 x Now $y(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})$ means x = $-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ and find y. Putting x = $-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ sin -1 y = cos -1 $(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})$ = $\frac{3\pi}{4}$ y (at x = $-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ ) = sin( $\frac{3\pi}{4}$ ) = $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$
questions.explanation_html:
Given $\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\frac{dy}{dx}+\sqrt{1-y^{2}}=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{\sqrt{1-y^{2}}}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{dy}{\sqrt{1-y^{2}}}+\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}=0$

$\Rightarrow$ sin-1 y + sin-1 x = c

Given that $y(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

So when x = $\frac{1}{2}$ then y = $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

$\therefore$ sin-1 $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ + sin-1 $\frac{1}{2}$ = c

$\Rightarrow$ c = $\frac{\pi}{3}$ + $\frac{\pi}{6}$ = $\frac{\pi}{2}$

So sin-1 y + sin-1 x = $\frac{\pi}{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ sin-1 y = $\frac{\pi}{2}$ - sin-1 x

$\Rightarrow$ sin-1 y = cos-1 x

Now $y(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})$ means x = $-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ and find y.

Putting x = $-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

sin-1 y = cos-1 $(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})$ = $\frac{3\pi}{4}$

y (at x = $-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ ) = sin( $\frac{3\pi}{4}$ ) = $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

questions.explanation_text: $\sqrt{1+x^{2}+y^{2}+x^{2}y^{2}}$ + xy $\frac{dy}{dx}$ = 0 $\Rightarrow$ $\sqrt{(1+x^{2})(1+y^{2})}$ + xy $\frac{dy}{dx}$ = 0 $\Rightarrow$ $\sqrt{(1+x^{2})}\sqrt{(1+y^{2})}$ = -xy $\frac{dy}{dx}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\int \frac{ydy}{\sqrt{1+y^{2}}}=-\int \frac{\sqrt{1+x^{2}}}{x}dx$ .....(1) Now put 1 + x 2 = u 2 and 1 + y 2 = v 2 2xdx = 2udu and 2ydy = 2vdv $\Rightarrow$ xdx = udu and ydy = vdv Substitute these values in equation (1) $\int \frac{vdv}{v}=-\int \frac{u^{2}du}{u^{2}-1}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\int dv=-\int \frac{u^{2}-1+1}{u^{2}-1}du$ $\Rightarrow$ v = $-\int (1+\frac{1}{u^{2}-1})du$ $\Rightarrow$ v = -u - $\frac{1}{2}log_{e}|\frac{u-1}{u+1}|$ + C $\Rightarrow$ $\sqrt{1+y^{2}}$ = $-\sqrt{1+x^{2}}$ + $\frac{1}{2}log_{e}|\frac{\sqrt{1+x^{2}}+1}{\sqrt{1+x^{2}}-1}|$ + C $\Rightarrow$ $\sqrt{1+y^{2}}+\sqrt{1+x^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}log_{e}(\frac{\sqrt{1+x^{2}}+1}{\sqrt{1+x^{2}}-1})+C$
questions.explanation_html:
$\sqrt{1+x^{2}+y^{2}+x^{2}y^{2}}$ + xy $\frac{dy}{dx}$ = 0

$\Rightarrow$ $\sqrt{(1+x^{2})(1+y^{2})}$ + xy $\frac{dy}{dx}$ = 0

$\Rightarrow$ $\sqrt{(1+x^{2})}\sqrt{(1+y^{2})}$ = -xy $\frac{dy}{dx}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\int \frac{ydy}{\sqrt{1+y^{2}}}=-\int \frac{\sqrt{1+x^{2}}}{x}dx$ .....(1)

Now put 1 + x2 = u2 and 1 + y2 = v2

2xdx = 2udu and 2ydy = 2vdv

$\Rightarrow$ xdx = udu and ydy = vdv

Substitute these values in equation (1)

$\int \frac{vdv}{v}=-\int \frac{u^{2}du}{u^{2}-1}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\int dv=-\int \frac{u^{2}-1+1}{u^{2}-1}du$

$\Rightarrow$ v = $-\int (1+\frac{1}{u^{2}-1})du$

$\Rightarrow$ v = -u - $\frac{1}{2}log_{e}|\frac{u-1}{u+1}|$ + C

$\Rightarrow$ $\sqrt{1+y^{2}}$ = $-\sqrt{1+x^{2}}$ + $\frac{1}{2}log_{e}|\frac{\sqrt{1+x^{2}}+1}{\sqrt{1+x^{2}}-1}|$ + C

$\Rightarrow$ $\sqrt{1+y^{2}}+\sqrt{1+x^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}log_{e}(\frac{\sqrt{1+x^{2}}+1}{\sqrt{1+x^{2}}-1})+C$

questions.explanation_text: $\frac{2+sinx}{y+1}.\frac{dy}{dx}=-cosx$ $\Rightarrow$ $\int \frac{dy}{y+1}=\int \frac{(-cosx)dx}{2+sinx}$ $\Rightarrow$ $ln|y+1|=-ln|2+sinx|+lnc$ $\Rightarrow$ $ln|(y+1)(2+sinx)|=lnc$ As y(0) = 1 $\therefore$ $ln|(1+1)(2+0)|=lnc$ $\Rightarrow$ $\therefore$ c = 4 $\therefore$ $(y+1)(2+sinx)$ = 4 $\Rightarrow$ y = $\frac{2-sinx}{2+sinx}$ Given y( $\pi$ ) = a $\therefore$ y( $\pi$ ) = $\frac{2-sin\pi}{2+sin\pi}$ = 1 = a $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{(2+sinx)(-cosx)-(2-sinx).(cosx)}{(2+sinx)^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{dy}{dx}|_{x=\pi}=$ 1 = b So, (a, b) = (1, 1)

As y(0) = 1

$\therefore$ $ln|(1+1)(2+0)|=lnc$

$\Rightarrow$ y = $\frac{2-sinx}{2+sinx}$

Given y( $\pi$ ) = a

$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{(2+sinx)(-cosx)-(2-sinx).(cosx)}{(2+sinx)^{2}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{dy}{dx}|_{x=\pi}=$ 1 = b

So, (a, b) = (1, 1)

questions.explanation_text: Given, $x\frac{dy}{dx}+2y=x^{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{dy}{dx}+(\frac{2}{x})y=x$ This is a linear differential equation. $\therefore$ I.F $=e^{\int \frac{2}{x}dx}$ $=e^{2lnx}$ $=x^{2}$ $\therefore$ Solution is, $y \cdot x^{2}=\int x \cdot x^{2}dx$ $\Rightarrow$ $yx^{2}=\frac{x^{4}}{4}+C$ given $y(1)=1$ $\therefore$ $1.1=\frac{4}{4}+C$ $\Rightarrow$ $C=\frac{3}{4}$ $\therefore$ Equation is $yx^{2}=\frac{x^{4}}{4}+\frac{3}{4}$ $\therefore$ $y(\frac{1}{2})$ means $x=\frac{1}{2}$ $\therefore$ $y \cdot (\frac{1}{2})^{2}=\frac{1}{4} \times (\frac{1}{2})^{4}+\frac{3}{4}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{y}{4}=\frac{1}{64}+\frac{3}{4}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{y}{4}=\frac{1+48}{64}$ $\Rightarrow$ y = $\frac{49}{16}$

$x\frac{dy}{dx}+2y=x^{2}$

$=e^{2lnx}$

$=x^{2}$

$\therefore$   Solution is,

$y \cdot x^{2}=\int x \cdot x^{2}dx$

$\Rightarrow$    $yx^{2}=\frac{x^{4}}{4}+C$

given   $y(1)=1$

$\therefore$    $1.1=\frac{4}{4}+C$

$\Rightarrow$    $C=\frac{3}{4}$

$\therefore$   Equation is

$yx^{2}=\frac{x^{4}}{4}+\frac{3}{4}$

$\therefore$    $y(\frac{1}{2})$   means    $x=\frac{1}{2}$

$\therefore$    $y \cdot (\frac{1}{2})^{2}=\frac{1}{4} \times (\frac{1}{2})^{4}+\frac{3}{4}$

$\Rightarrow$    $\frac{y}{4}=\frac{1}{64}+\frac{3}{4}$

$\Rightarrow$     $\frac{y}{4}=\frac{1+48}{64}$

$\Rightarrow$   y = $\frac{49}{16}$

questions.explanation_text: We have $y=c_{1}e^{c_{2}x}$ $\Rightarrow y^{'}=c_{1}c_{2}e^{c_{2}x}=c_{2}y$ $\Rightarrow \frac{y^{'}}{y}=c_{2}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{y^{''}y(y^{'})^{2}}{y^{2}}=0$ $\Rightarrow y^{''}y=(y^{'})^{2}$

questions.question_text: The solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x+y}{x}$ satisfying the condition $y(1)=1$ is :
questions.question_html:
The solution of the differential equation

$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x+y}{x}$ satisfying the condition $y(1)=1$ is :
questions.explanation_text: $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x+y}{x}=1+\frac{y}{x}$ Putting $y=$ $vx$ and $\frac{dy}{dx}=v+x\frac{dv}{dx}$ we get $v+x\frac{dv}{dx}=1+v$ $\Rightarrow \int \frac{dx}{x}=\int dv$ $\Rightarrow v=lnx+c$ $\Rightarrow y=xlnx+cx$ As $y(1)=1$ $\therefore$ $c=1$ So solution is $y=xlnx+x$
questions.explanation_html:
$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x+y}{x}=1+\frac{y}{x}$

Putting $y=$ $vx$

and $\frac{dy}{dx}=v+x\frac{dv}{dx}$

we get

$v+x\frac{dv}{dx}=1+v$

$\Rightarrow \int \frac{dx}{x}=\int dv$

$\Rightarrow v=lnx+c$

$\Rightarrow y=xlnx+cx$

As $y(1)=1$

$\therefore$ $c=1$

So solution is $y=xlnx+x$

questions.question_text: The differential equation of all circles passing through the origin and having their centres on the $x$ -axis is :
questions.question_html: The differential equation of all circles passing through the origin and having their centres on the $x$ -axis is :
questions.explanation_text: General equation of circles passing through origin and having their centres on the $x$ -axis is $x^{2}+y^{2}+2gx=0....(i)$ On differentiating $w.r.t.x,$ we get $2x+2y.\frac{dy}{dx}+2g=0$ $\Rightarrow g=-(x+y\frac{dy}{dx})$ $\therefore$ equation $(i)$ be $x^{2}+y^{2}+2{-(x+y\frac{dy}{dx})}x=0$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}-2x^{2}-2x\frac{dy}{dx}.y=0$ $\Rightarrow y^{2}=x^{2}+2xy\frac{dy}{dx}$
questions.explanation_html:
General equation of circles passing through origin

and having their centres on the $x$ -axis is

$x^{2}+y^{2}+2gx=0....(i)$

On differentiating $w.r.t.x,$ we get

$2x+2y.\frac{dy}{dx}+2g=0$

$\Rightarrow g=-(x+y\frac{dy}{dx})$

$\therefore$ equation $(i)$ be

$x^{2}+y^{2}+2{-(x+y\frac{dy}{dx})}x=0$

$\Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}-2x^{2}-2x\frac{dy}{dx}.y=0$

$\Rightarrow y^{2}=x^{2}+2xy\frac{dy}{dx}$

questions.question_text: If $x\frac{dy}{dx}=y(logy-logx+1),$ then the solution of the equation is :
questions.question_html: If $x\frac{dy}{dx}=y(logy-logx+1),$ then the solution of the equation is :
questions.explanation_text: $\frac{xdy}{dx}=y(logy-logx+1)$ $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y}{x}(log(\frac{y}{x})+1)$ Put $y=vx$ $\frac{dy}{dx}=v+\frac{xdv}{dx}$ $\Rightarrow v+\frac{xdv}{dx}=v(logv+1)$ $\frac{xdv}{dx}=vlogv$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dv}{vlogv}=\frac{dx}{x}$ Put $logv=z$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{v}dv=dz$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dz}{x}=\frac{dx}{x}$ $\Rightarrow lnz=lnx+lnc$ $x=cx$ or $logv=cx$ or $log(\frac{y}{x})=cx.$
questions.explanation_html:
$\frac{xdy}{dx}=y(logy-logx+1)$

$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y}{x}(log(\frac{y}{x})+1)$

Put $y=vx$

$\frac{dy}{dx}=v+\frac{xdv}{dx}$

$\Rightarrow v+\frac{xdv}{dx}=v(logv+1)$

$\frac{xdv}{dx}=vlogv$

$\Rightarrow \frac{dv}{vlogv}=\frac{dx}{x}$

Put $logv=z$

$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{v}dv=dz$

$\Rightarrow \frac{dz}{x}=\frac{dx}{x}$

$\Rightarrow lnz=lnx+lnc$

$x=cx$ or $logv=cx$

or $log(\frac{y}{x})=cx.$

questions.question_text: The differential equation for the family of circle $x^{2}+y^{2}-2ay=0,$ where a is an arbitrary constant is :
questions.question_html: The differential equation for the family of circle $x^{2}+y^{2}-2ay=0,$ where a is an arbitrary constant is :
questions.explanation_text: $x^{2}+y^{2}-2ay=0...(1)$ Differentiate, $2x+2y\frac{dy}{dx}-2a\frac{dy}{dx}=0$ $\Rightarrow a=\frac{x+yy^{'}}{y^{'}}$ Put in $(1),$ $x^{2}+y^{2}-2(\frac{x+yy^{'}}{y^{'}})=y=0$ $\Rightarrow (x^{2}+y^{2})y^{'}-2xy-2y^{2}y^{'}=0$ $\Rightarrow (x^{2}-y^{2})y^{'}=2xy$
questions.explanation_html:
$x^{2}+y^{2}-2ay=0...(1)$

Differentiate,

$2x+2y\frac{dy}{dx}-2a\frac{dy}{dx}=0$

$\Rightarrow a=\frac{x+yy^{'}}{y^{'}}$

Put in $(1),$ $x^{2}+y^{2}-2(\frac{x+yy^{'}}{y^{'}})=y=0$

$\Rightarrow (x^{2}+y^{2})y^{'}-2xy-2y^{2}y^{'}=0$

$\Rightarrow (x^{2}-y^{2})y^{'}=2xy$

questions.question_text: Solution of the differential equation $ydx+(x+x^{2}y)dy=0$ is
questions.question_html: Solution of the differential equation $ydx+(x+x^{2}y)dy=0$ is
questions.explanation_text: $ydx+(x+x^{2}y)dy=0$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dx}{dy}=-\frac{x}{y}-x^{2}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dx}{dy}+\frac{x}{y}=-x^{2},$ It is Bernoullis form. Divide by $x^{2}$ $x^{-2}\frac{dx}{dy}+x^{-1}(\frac{1}{y})=-1.$ put $x^{-1}=t,-x^{-2}\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{dt}{dy}$ We get, $-\frac{dt}{dy}+t(\frac{1}{y})=-1$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dt}{dy}-(\frac{1}{y})t=1$ It is linear in $t.$ Integrating factor $=e^{\int -\frac{1}{y}dy}=e^{-logy}=y^{-1}$ $\therefore$ Solution is $t(y^{-1})=\int (y^{-1})dy+c$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{x}.\frac{1}{y}=logy+c$ $\Rightarrow logy-\frac{1}{xy}=c$
questions.explanation_html:
$ydx+(x+x^{2}y)dy=0$

$\Rightarrow \frac{dx}{dy}=-\frac{x}{y}-x^{2}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{dx}{dy}+\frac{x}{y}=-x^{2},$

It is Bernoullis form. Divide by $x^{2}$

$x^{-2}\frac{dx}{dy}+x^{-1}(\frac{1}{y})=-1.$

put $x^{-1}=t,-x^{-2}\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{dt}{dy}$

We get, $-\frac{dt}{dy}+t(\frac{1}{y})=-1$

$\Rightarrow \frac{dt}{dy}-(\frac{1}{y})t=1$

It is linear in $t.$

Integrating factor

$=e^{\int -\frac{1}{y}dy}=e^{-logy}=y^{-1}$

$\therefore$ Solution is

$t(y^{-1})=\int (y^{-1})dy+c$

$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{x}.\frac{1}{y}=logy+c$

$\Rightarrow logy-\frac{1}{xy}=c$

The solution of the differential equation

$(1+y^{2})+(x-e^{tan^{-1}y})\frac{dy}{dx}=0,$ is :

$(1+y^{2})+(x-e^{tan^{-1}y})\frac{dy}{dx}=0$

$\Rightarrow \frac{dx}{dy}+\frac{x}{(1+y^{2})}=\frac{e^{tan^{-1}y}}{(1+y^{2})}$

$I.F=e^{\int \frac{1}{(1+y^{2})}dy}=e^{tan^{-1}y}$

$x(e^{tan^{-1}y})=\int \frac{e^{tan^{-1}y}}{1+y^{2}}e^{tan^{-1}y}dy$

$x(e^{tan^{-1}y})=\frac{e^{2tan^{-1}y}}{2}+C$

$\therefore$ $2xe^{tan^{-1}y}=e^{2tan^{-1}y}+k$
